items.cleanReaderHtml:
Imagine feline forms haunting every human face you encounter as you go about your day. Seeing these Cheshire cats flickering into view, you might think you had tumbled down the rabbit hole. It seems phantasmagorical. But this is the experience of a 28-year-old man named Karl who lives in the northeastern United States.

When Karl wakes in the morning, his gray tabby Luna is often the first being he greets, and Luna’s face, the first he gazes upon: the whiskers, the almond eyes, the pink nose, the stripes. When this happens, the image of Luna’s face sticks with him for several hours or even the rest of his day. He sees his feline companion’s eyes and silver stripes superimposed over all of the human faces that he glimpses, both in person and online.

The reverse is also true: If the first face he sees in the morning is a human one, he will see that person’s pupils and eye shape superimposed on every other face he sees that day, including the furry mug of his pet cat. These superpositions are seamless: The faces otherwise appear normal and coherent.

Karl’s visions began after he had brain surgery to remove some abnormally connected blood vessels from his right posterior temporal lobe, the command center for recognizing a person’s identity and reading their facial expressions. These visions, and more run-of-the-mill face distortions, where faces simply don't look right, have plagued Karl for two years post-surgery. He appears to have developed a combination of two rare neurological conditions: palinopsia, where an image persists in someone’s field of vision after exposure, and prosopometamorphopsia, where a person sees distorted faces.

Brad Duchaine, a professor and psychologist at Dartmouth University, heard about Karl through Jennifer Nosker, a neuropsychologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital who worked with Karl after his surgery. When Karl told Nosker about his face distortions, she found Duchaine’s work on the subject, and contacted him. At Dartmouth’s Social Perception Lab, Duchaine has been studying prosopometamorphopsia for many years, collecting accounts through a website dedicated to the condition. Over the past five years, around 275 individuals have contacted the lab through the site .

“Karl finds the transfers between cat and human faces very strange,” writes Duchaine, in an email. “He has had problems with face perception for some time, though, so he has adapted to them and takes them in stride.” All of his distortions began after his surgery, Duchaine explains.

Duchaine and Nosker recently published a case study about Karl in the journal Cortex together with a third colleague, Antonio Mello, a psychologist at Dartmouth.

Ordinarily, people with prosopometamorphopsia see alterations in the shape or position of facial features or in the color or texture of skin. For example, some people with the condition see eyes and mouths stretched into “demonic” shapes, with grooves in the forehead, or they might see features drooping, swelling or twisting. Face substitutions are an atypical expression of this unusual condition.

One of the earliest documented cases of face substitution in the scientific literature also involved a pet: a poodle. According to a case study published in Cortex in 1986, a woman known as “patient 2” was riding a bus about 9 months after a stroke when she saw a poodle in the lap of another passenger. After she looked away from the dog, however, she noticed everyone else in the bus seemed to suddenly have the poodle’s face in place of their human one. This visual hallucination continued for another 30 minutes, even after she got off the bus.

At the time, the implications of her experience seemed quite shocking: Her visions suggested that the brain processes faces differently from other categories of visual stimuli, an idea that is now widely accepted. Studies have found that the fusiform gyrus, a region of the temporal lobe, becomes active when a person is looking at faces, and only faces.

The cases of Karl and patient 2 differ in at least two ways, wrote Duchaine. “First, the woman in the 1986 case saw the poodle’s whole face on the bus passengers, but Karl sees only parts carried over, mainly the eyes and pupils. Second, the 1986 transfer went one way, from dog to human. Karl’s goes both ways. If he sees his cat first, its eyes appear on people. If he sees a person first, that person’s eyes can appear on his cat.”

In their recent analysis, Duchaine and his colleagues used artificial intelligence to generate photorealistic versions of the visions that both Karl and patient 2 might have experienced. Karl helped to revise the cat-human hybrids to match his experience, while the poodle heads were generated using line drawings made in 1986.

The images are reminiscent of the works of Matthew Grabelsky , a contemporary American artist who creates hyperrealistic oil paintings of humans with animal heads riding the New York City subway, and surrealist painter and novelist Leonora Carrington , who incorporated horse-headed women and other human-animal hybrids into her works.

Karl and patient 2 remind us that our perception of faces crosses species lines. If a single region of the brain is fundamentally wired to recognize faces in both people as well as cats and dogs, this ability may share a common anatomical blueprint that dates back hundreds of millions of years. It might even help explain why we are so quick to attribute human emotions and personalities to the other creatures with whom we share the planet and our homes.

items.title: RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act
items.author: Greg Werkheiser
items.summary: The Act survived Republican and Democratic administrations, recessions, and wars, but its health declined precipitously this year after a devastating bout of congressional malpractice. There’s still time to save it.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Greg Werkheiser
RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act

videos.caption: Enlace audiovisual citado en la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the beloved American law that spent six decades giving communities a voice in federal decisions affecting the places that tell their stories, died shortly after its birthday following a brief but devastating bout of congressional malpractice. It was 60.

Born on October 15, 1966, with unanimous bipartisan support and signed into law by then-President Lyndon B. Johnson, NHPA was conceived in response to a national epidemic of federally sponsored demolition. Americans discovered that an astonishing 50% of the nation’s 12,000 historic buildings and landmarks documented in an inventory begun by the Civil Works Administration in 1933 had been demolished amid federally supported urban renewal and highway development — a breathtaking path of destruction dubbed “the death mask of America.”

NHPA’s central proposition was modest: Before the federal government or a developer damaged or destroyed an important part of America’s heritage, it simply needed to stop, look, and listen.

items.title: Who Gets Remembered in Art History? New Free Online Course Explores Women Who Shaped Indonesian Art
items.author: National Gallery Singapore
items.summary: Co-developed by National Gallery Singapore and independent curator Alia Swastika, the course foregrounds women’s contributions to Indonesian art.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
How have women artists shaped Indonesia's cultural, social, and artistic histories? National Gallery Singapore's new free online course, Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower, co-developed with independent curator Alia Swastika, explores this question through the practices and perspectives of leading contemporary artists.   

“The absence of women [in historical accounts] does not necessarily indicate a lack of participation.” — Alia Swastika

The course underscores the importance of recovering women’s contributions and bringing overlooked figures and landmark events into view. 

Through the work of artists from different generations, regions, and artistic backgrounds, Art and Women in Indonesia highlights a plurality of experiences and perspectives, offering new ways of understanding Indonesia’s histories and their continued resonance in the present. 

Structured over five weeks, the course explores the practices of six artists and one collective whose work spans painting, sculpture, installation, performances, and collaborative forms. Together, they illuminate the diverse ways women have contributed to Indonesia’s cultural landscape while engaging questions of memory, power, gender, spirituality, and resistance. 

Featured artists include Arahmaiani and Dolorosa Sinaga, whose works confront authoritarianism, censorship, conservatism, and the politics of the female body in public space. Through distinct artistic approaches, they expose the mechanisms through which women’s lives are regulated while fostering critical engagement with urgent social and political issues.  

 Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower also examines how Nunung WS, Titarubi, and Bakudapan Food Study Group navigate the relationship between individual experience and collective histories. Through installation, abstraction, and collaborative practices, they explore motherhood, cultural memory, care, and everyday labor as ways of engaging with broader social and political structures.  

Drawing on Balinese cosmologies and visual traditions, Citra Sasmita and Mangku Muriati foreground female protagonists and goddesses, reworking inherited narratives and transforming painting into a site for feminist interpretation and historical reflection.  

Accompanied by exclusive video interviews, readings, and discussion activities, the course provides deeper insight into the artists’ practices and the contexts from which they emerge. It also invites participants to reconsider the role of women in art history and to reflect on how art shapes the histories we remember, the narratives we inherit, and the futures we imagine. 

 Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower is part of National Gallery Singapore’s series of Online Courses on Southeast Asian Art. Join a growing global community of learners in exploring stories of women, art, and social change in and beyond Indonesia. 

Register for free at nationalgallery.sg.

items.title: SpaceX Catches the Upper Stage of Its Starship for the First Time, Making the Company One Step Closer to a Reusable Rocket
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: After circling the Earth 14 times, the upper portion of Starship descended to the planet's surface and was caught by a giant pair of robotic, chopstick-like arms. However, the company failed to snatch the lower stage, which it had previously demonstrated

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sara Hashemi
Sara Hashemi

items.cleanReaderHtml:
On November 14, SpaceX successfully caught the separated upper section of its massive Starship rocket as it returned from Earth orbit, marking a historic step toward the development of reusable rockets.

“That was the missing link,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during a livestream of the landing, reports Mike Wall at Space.com . “That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes.”

The 407-foot rocket launched for its 15th test flight from the company’s Starbase site in southern Texas on November 13. The lower stage, called the Super Heavy booster, separated during the ascent after providing the thrust needed for takeoff. The upper stage, called the Starship spacecraft, went on to complete a roughly 22.5-hour journey, which involved 14 laps around Earth and the deployment of 26 Starlink satellites.

After that, the spacecraft navigated back to Starbase, where a giant pair of robotic, chopstick-like arms captured it.

“Can you believe it?” Huot said during the livestream, reports Marcia Dunn for the Associated Press . “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”

Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement! https://t.co/YJzmGUZb2B

Not everything happened as planned, however. The company had also hoped to catch Super Heavy , which it has previously done three times, per the AP. This time around, the booster had to be diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico because of low fuel. SpaceX is investigating what triggered the issue, according to a statement .

Still, snatching the upper stage is harder than grabbing the booster, since the Starship spacecraft travels higher and faster than the lower stage, according to Space.com . The historic catch brings SpaceX closer to its goal of building a fully reusable rocket. The company wants to build a rocket system that can travel to space and back with minimal refurbishments needed between launches.

“If every time you drove somewhere you had to throw away the car, you’d be [like] ‘wow, that’s a crazy car where you have to throw away after every time you drive it.’ But that’s how it works for rockets,” said SpaceX CEO Elon Musk at the X Takeover 2025 event, reports Matthew Glasser at ABC News .

Being able to reuse rockets would drastically cut down the cost of launching objects into space, says Casey Dreier , chief of space policy for the Planetary Society, to the outlet. It also “allows you to increase the amount of stuff you can send into space, which SpaceX has really been leaning into.”

Starship only recently reached Earth orbit . It passed the milestone on September 28, during a test flight in which the spacecraft looped around the planet twice. However, it returned sooner than planned because one of its engines had shut down.

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman took to social media to congratulate the company on its feat, writing “it was almost like magic.” The space agency will test Starship during the Artemis 3 mission, slated for mid-2027, when SpaceX and aerospace company Blue Origin compete to provide the lunar lander NASA will use to take humans back to the moon, planned for the following year.

However, significant technical challenges remain. SpaceX still needs to demonstrate in-orbit fuel transfers —something that has never been done before—since Starship is too heavy to launch with the fuel needed to reach the moon.

Mission teams have already started gathering data for next steps, reports Jackie Wattles for CNN . Now, the company’s analysts and engineers can look at how the rocket held up during its journey—and importantly, how the heat shield fared during its scorching re-entry into the atmosphere—and find ways to improve its performance. A SpaceX spokesperson told the outlet earlier last week that the company intends to be reliably reusing Starship vehicles by the time astronauts return to the lunar surface.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Whether showcasing a prized possession or peering through a spyglass to navigate open water, Juliet Schreckinger’s curious characters work together and form unexpected alliances. Personalities like Oscar the Octopus and Quinn the Sperm Whale recur in the artist’s ink and graphite drawings, and her most recent series comprises the show Limitless Sea at Arch Enemy Arts.

Schreckinger’s marine and woodland critters adopt a playful, cartoonish air, like personalities in a children’s book who find themselves adrift and in need of a friend. Lighthouses, lanterns, and rays of sun breaking through clouds glow with optimism. And while an overarching narrative may be murky, the unlikely companions and cooperative activities illuminate dreamlike scenes that encourage inquisitiveness and joy.

An undercurrent of persistence and hope also runs through Limited Sea, mirroring the artist’s recent healing process after a major surgery. It’s “a show made up of characters navigating through the foggy darkness by focusing on the light…and on the other side is limitless possibility,” Schreckinger says in a statement. As she navigated her own challenges—including making this series with only one good eye—these works served as a reminder of what’s most important: “finding the beauty, finding the light, and spending time with those who make your soul happy,” she says.

Limitless Sea continues through November 29 in Philadelphia. Schreckinger’s work will also be on view next month in General Strike 2, an exhibition of artist matchboxes, at Joy Machine. See more on Schreckinger’s Instagram.

items.title: The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles Elimination Status, Which It's Held for 26 Years. Cases Have Now Surged to the Highest Levels in Decades
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: So far this year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed more than 5,400 measles cases—the highest annual total since 1991—and 43 outbreaks. Dropping vaccination rates are likely to blame

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News

Sarah Kuta
Sarah Kuta

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The United States has lost its measles elimination status as cases surge to the highest levels in decades.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), an international public health agency for the Americas, has concluded that the U.S. no longer meets the criteria for measles elimination, according to the Wall Street Journal ’s Liz Essley Whyte and Jennifer Calfas.

“Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system,” Demetre Daskalakis , a former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), tells CNN ’s Brenda Goodman. “It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges.”

Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning there had been no continuous spread of the disease for more than 12 months. However, in recent years, the highly contagious viral disease has made a comeback.

So far this year, the CDC has confirmed more than 5,400 measles cases—the highest annual total since 1991 —and 43 outbreaks. According to CDC data, 96 percent of those cases involved individuals who were not vaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. At least ten individuals have died from the disease this year, with deaths occurring in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

“Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage,” Noel Brewer , a public health researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and chair of a committee that reports on U.S. measles activity to the PAHO, tells the Wall Street Journal . “We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. It typically causes a high fever, cough, runny nose and distinctive rash, but it can also lead to serious complications, including pneumonia, blindness, brain swelling and, in some cases, death. The first measles vaccine was authorized for public use in 1963.

The CDC recommends children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine, which is 97 percent effective at thwarting measles. At least 95 percent of the population needs to be vaccinated to prevent the disease from spreading. However, vaccination rates have fallen in recent years. During the 2025-2026 school year, 92.4 percent of kindergartners had received the MMR vaccine, down from 95.2 percent in 2019-2020, according to CDC data .

In January, the CDC overhauled the U.S.’s childhood immunization schedule , reducing the number of diseases it recommends that all American children should be vaccinated against to 11, down from 17 a month earlier. The MMR vaccine was still suggested for all kids.

“It’s a very sad moment,” Anne Schuchat , an epidemiologist and a former deputy director of the CDC, tells KFF Health News ’ Amy Maxmen. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.”

As viruses spread and replicate, small genetic differences accumulate, creating subtle variations in their genetic makeup. By comparing the genetic sequences of viruses collected during an outbreak, researchers can trace the relationships between different outbreaks and assess whether they likely stemmed from the same chain of transmission.

According to Nextstrain , a public database that tracks pathogen evolution, an outbreak that started in Texas in 2025 spread to Utah and Arizona, where the virus continued circulating for more than a year.

“There’s a general pattern of outbreaks seeding other outbreaks,” J.T. McCrone , an evolutionary biologist at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center who helps oversee Nextstrain, tells the New York Times ’ Apoorva Mandavilli. “Measles is very contagious; it spreads very easily. We have a lot of connected communities in the U.S., and so you can hop from population to population and maintain a transmission chain.”

Measles has re-emerged as a public health challenge around the world. Canada lost its measles-elimination status in November 2025, followed by the United Kingdom in January 2026. Spain, Austria, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan also lost their status .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Molecules that waft from breath, skin and urine can hold clues to Parkinson’s, cancer and other ills. Scientists hope to harness these signatures for non-invasive medical tests

Cholera “Tramples the victors & the vanquished both.” Collection: Images from the History of Medicine (IHM) Author(s): Seymour, Robert, 1798-1836, artist Publication: [London] : , [October 1, 1831] Language(s): English Format: Still image Subject(s): Death Abstract: Cholera, as a large shrouded specter with skeletal hands and feet, indiscriminately crushes soldiers on both sides of the battlefield. Copyright: The National Library of Medicine believes this item to be in the public domain. (More information) Extent: 1 print : 10 x 12 cm. Provenance: Purchase; 1967. Technique: lithograph, color NLM Unique ID: 101393375 (See catalog record) NLM Image ID: A021774 Permanent Link: http://resource.nlm.nih.gov/101393375

This story was originally published by Knowable Magazine .

When social anthropologist Hanna Marie Ihlebæk interviewed nurses at a Norwegian cancer ward for her PhD thesis, she was surprised to learn that many of them relied on their sense of smell in their work. “Urine infection is really distinct, I can recognize that smell in the corridor!” one of the nurses said. Another claimed to be able to pick out digestive bleeding and cell necrosis. “I don’t know what I would have done without my ability to smell,” said a third.

Long ago, in the 5th century BCE, the Greek physician-philosopher Hippocrates held that disease could be identified by body odor. In modern times, we have stories of Oscar the cat who seemed to perceive which residents would soon pass away at a Rhode Island nursing home, and dogs that have been used to detect bladder cancer, malaria and Covid-19. In Africa, giant pouched rats are employed to sniff out tuberculosis.

For years, scientists have been exploring how the molecules that waft from our breath or skin might be harnessed to sniff out a laundry list of diseases — Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, certain cancers, the flu and the common cold. Yet the field has struggled to bring such tests to the clinic. Now, with new tools that can detect tiny amounts of molecules, as well as advances in machine learning , that goal appears within reach. A variety of ailments might soon be efficiently diagnosed with non-invasive tests that employ devices as simple as Breathalyzers.

“It’s really, really exciting,” says Mark Woollam, a chemical biologist at the University of Indianapolis.

A handful of breath-based tests are already in use , such as one that detects gastric infection by Helicobacter pylori , a major cause of stomach ulcers. Patients drink a solution spiked with urea containing a “heavy” version of carbon; if H. pylori is present, the bacterium will use the urea to make carbon dioxide and the test will detect that heavy-carbon CO 2 in the patients’ breath. But tests like that require swallowing a special substance and shipping a sample to a lab for analysis. Today, researchers are also working to develop tests that could give results directly at home, or at a doctor’s office. They are designed to sniff out volatile organic compounds, or VOCs. Such compounds are mostly in gas form at room temperature and can be emitted from breath, sweat, urine, blood and fecal matter.

To collect breath for analysis, for example, volunteers breathe into small, lab-grade plastic bags that resemble juice pouches, or into syringe-like breath samplers. Such samples are then analyzed in a lab with a technique called gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Other tests employ cheaper and more portable electronic noses, which are made of a series of sensors that can pick out various molecules.

Figuring out what molecules are significant and what conclusions can be drawn from an individual sample makes the development of such tests “very, very challenging,” Woollam says. Breath can contain contaminants from the surrounding air (think pollution or cigarette smoke), and the composition of breath can vary from one moment to another, making it hard to standardize tests and interpret single measurements. “From sitting to lying, you change your breath profile. You hold your breath, you change your breath profile. You take a drug, you change your breath profile… So how do you want to sort that out?” says chemist Wolfram Miekisch , of the University Medical Center Rostock in Germany.

But researchers have made progress in pinpointing molecules that are markers of specific diseases. When tumors grow, for example, oxidative stress in the body increases, which leads to the breakdown of fatty molecules within cells into smaller, volatile compounds, Woollam says. One study that tested the breath of patients before and after a surgery to remove lung tumors identified 16 such compounds that might serve as lung cancer breath biomarkers, including pentanal, foul-smelling butyric acid, woody hexanal and decanal, which smells like orange peel. In other research, analyses of molecules emitted from melanoma biopsy samples suggested that compounds such as the pungent chemical called 4-methyl decane could serve as a biomarker.

Molecules in urine could also offer clues to cancer. Woollam and colleagues analyzed molecules wafting from the urine of men undergoing a prostate cancer biopsy and found that a panel of six molecules could detect the disease in 75 percent of cases. While it’s less sensitive than the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood-based test, the VOC method gave fewer false positives, which could help patients avoid unnecessary treatment.

Some cancer tests based on volatile compounds emanating from urine may soon hit the market. One such test by the biotech company TOBY, named after the trail-sniffing dog in Sherlock Holmes books, is designed to detect bladder cancer. Rather than looking for a single biomarker, TOBY’s test uses AI to analyze patterns of molecules wafting from urine. It was granted Breakthrough Device designation (which can speed up approval) by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2026, validating its potential; its developers say it is about a year away from commercial launch. The TOBY team is also working on a similar test for Alzheimer’s, which received the FDA’s Breakthrough Device designation in May.

Clues to disease also reside in sebum, an oily, sticky substance produced by tiny glands in hair follicles. Researchers are investigating the link between volatiles emanating from sebum and Parkinson’s disease, which tends to be diagnosed late, meaning patients go longer without their symptoms being properly managed.

items.title: Ancient Humans May Have Hunted Hippos With Poisoned Spear Tips on the Arabian Peninsula 125,000 Years Ago
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: A new study suggests people hunted and processed game near a large, lush, freshwater lake in what is now southern Saudi Arabia, challenging the assumption that humans just passed through the region

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
Sarah Kuta

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Today, southern Saudi Arabia is a hot, dry desert, with sand dunes as far as the eye can see. But 125,000 years ago, it was home to a lush, freshwater lake that supported animals like hippopotamuses, buffalo, ostriches, camels, gazelles and oryx.

A new study, published November 12 in the journal Science , suggests that ancient humans took advantage of this rich biodiversity—and may even have created poisoned weapons to take down their prey.

Researchers conducted excavations at a Middle Paleolithic site known as Uruq Aljelibah, which means “sand dunes of a watering hole.” It’s located in the Empty Quarter, or Rub' al-Khali , a vast desert region spanning southern Saudi Arabia, as well as parts of Yemen, Oman and the United Arab Emirates. The evidence suggests the site was once home to a 131-square-mile lake that measured nearly 100 feet deep and was surrounded by palms, reeds, trees, shrubs and other plants, per a statement .

While investigating the site, archaeologists discovered more than 500 fossilized animal remains and more than 5,500 stone tools and artifacts, including stone points they think may have been dipped in poison to paralyze or kill big game.

The weapons were clustered near animal bones, which suggests the lakeshore was used for hunting and processing game. They also showed damage consistent with striking large animals, and some still had microscopic traces of animal tissue near their tips. Several also had chemical biomarkers associated with the arrow-poison tree ( Acokanthera schimperi ), a plant that contains cardiac glycosides , naturally occurring compounds that can affect heart rate.

The researchers also found hints of resin and fibers at the bases of the stone points, which suggests they were “hafted”—composite weapons made from multiple materials, rather than simple handheld tools.

“Hafting is often inferred indirectly, based on size and shape of stone tools, for instance,” study co-author Huw Groucutt , an archaeologist at the University of Malta, tells Haaretz ’s Ruth Schuster. “What we have done is find direct evidence in the form of residues showing how the tools were hafted and used, at a scale that is rarely applied in archaeology, and certainly not at sites like this, open air sites in arid regions.”

The scientists also discovered evidence of cutting, scraping and fiber processing, which suggests the people living here were exploiting plant resources for food, tools and binding materials.

“Early humans were far more technologically sophisticated than the surviving archaeological record often suggests,” lead author Chris Clarkson , an archaeologist at Griffith University, tells Gizmodo ’s Gayoung Lee. “We’re only beginning to understand just how complex their lives were.”

It’s rare for archaeologists to find stone tools and animal bones at the same site on the Arabian Peninsula. This one, however, has “thousands of artifacts on an old lakeshore alongside hippo, buffalo and ostrich, and some of the flakes fit back together, so the tools were made on the spot,” Jeffrey Rose , an archaeologist at the University of Algarve who was not involved with the research, tells Live Science ’s Charles Q. Choi. “It’s valuable new data.”

The site itself has been dated to 125,000 years ago; however, researchers haven’t definitively dated the stone points. That’s because they found all of the stone artifacts on the surface, not in layers of sediment that can be dated. They also don’t know whether the poison was effective, or how it was prepared.

Last year, researchers in northern Saudi Arabia’s Nefud Desert discovered 130 life-size engravings of animals likely dating to between 11,400 and 12,800 years ago. The animals depicted include camels, ibex, wild donkeys, gazelles and aurochs, an extinct ancestor of cattle.

But if the stone points are confirmed to be 125,000 years old, they would be the oldest poisoned hunting weapons ever identified by a considerable margin. The oldest discovered so far date to around 60,000 years ago .

The archaeologists did not find any human remains at the site, though they suspect it was inhabited by Homo sapiens .

items.title: Scientists Just Found Something Strange Under the Skin of Sea Pigs
items.author: David Nield
items.summary: A rare, detailed look at an unusual deep-sea creature The post Scientists Just Found Something Strange Under the Skin of Sea Pigs appeared first on Nautilus .

images.caption: Lámina de Nautilus
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The translucent blobs of flesh that are sea pigs are some of the most unusual sights in the deep ocean. They’re also difficult to study. Some of them live more than 32,800 feet below the surface, so getting eyes on them isn’t easy.

Now researchers have made a new discovery about the microbes that call these sea pigs home. Having symbiotic bacteria living under the skin isn’t unusual for these types of creatures, but a recent study published in ISME Host Microbe details what could be a new species and a new genus of such bacteria.

Read more: “ What Do You Know About the Deep-Sea Barbie Pig? ”

The microbes were found in eight sea pigs collected off the northern coast of Japan in the Northwest Pacific, and they dominated the body walls of the echinoderms—76.4 to 98.9 percent of the bacterial DNA found under the skin was this new species.

“Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria’s location within host tissues,” study author Yu Yoshida explained in a statement .

Not only is the bacteria new, it’s rather strange as well. It has a stripped-down genome (set of DNA instructions), and yet, it’s still capable of producing giant proteins to carry out work inside cells. The biggest protein the researchers found was 5,475 amino acids long, compared to around 300 for an average bacterial protein.

The study team has suggested Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola for the name of the new species, which roughly translates as the “abyss-dweller that lives in Scotoplanes ” ( Scotoplanes being the genus of the sea pig).

So what does this mean for the jelly-like sea pigs, which waddle along at the bottom of the ocean, picking up dead bits of matter with their tubular feet? Well, we’re not sure. The assumption is they have some kind of mutually beneficial relationship that’s not yet obvious to us.

This much we do know, though: For the inhabitants of the deep ocean, sea pigs are a vital part of the ecosystem. They recycle nutrients and protect other marine life against predators, which is why scientists are keen to learn more about how they thrive and how they’ve evolved.

“We’d really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and the effects on the host,” added Yoshida.

Of course, another literal deep dive will be needed to find out more.

Lead Image: Hajime Itoh/The University of Tokyo/CC BY 4.0

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .

And their genomes suggest they’ve adapted to the toxic conditions

items.title: Catwalks and crackdowns
items.author: Parisa Khoshnami
items.summary: Women in Tehran are changing society by dressing as they choose, in numbers too large to stop. This is the ‘art of presence’ - by Parisa Khoshnami Read on Aeon

images.caption: Two young women with red hair, one on a phone, in front of a wall covered with various drawings and a sign in Persian.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
At a café in downtown Tehran, Iran, on 11 September 2026. Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/via Getty Images

is an Iranian writer who lives in Paris, France. Her work has appeared in The New Statesman , BBC Persian, Euronews Persian as well as in Iranian journals.

Yasaman* is one of the regulars on Iranshahr, the new fashion hub of Tehran. Most evenings, she sets up a stall on the pavement and sells her drawings of manga and anime characters. On social media, she sports her own manga-inspired look: pink hair, pink mouth and smudgy pink eyeshadow extending beyond the corner of each eye. She tells her followers that, before she leaves her house, her mother says: ‘Put on less makeup.’ ‘Mum, be reasonable,’ she answers. ‘I’m going to Iranshahr. For Iranshahr this is nothing. I’m going to Paris Fashion Week. You know everyone there is doing a catwalk.’

Iranshahr’s sidewalks teem with young people parading the latest fashions and filming other young, stylish people for their social media feeds. This is where the fashionistas congregate, hanging out in cafés and galleries, and mingling on the sidewalks. Barely a headscarf is visible. The streets looked nothing like this a few years ago, but once the American-Israeli attacks began in February this year, the Islamic Republic has been fighting for its survival: with much of its leadership killed, the Strait of Hormuz under siege, and many of the country’s neighbours in league with the enemy, policing what people wear has slipped a long way down its list of priorities.

The hijab law has been codified in Iran since 1983, enforced nationwide by the ‘morality’ police. Disobeying it meant fines, flogging or imprisonment. But then one act of disobedience changed everything. In December 2017, Vida Movahed, a woman in her 30s, climbed onto a utility box on Enghelab Street in Tehran, took off her white headscarf and held it up on a stick. Although she was arrested and later sentenced to a year in prison, her action proved contagious. Other women climbed up onto boxes and makeshift plinths in the same street, waving their headscarves in the air. People began calling them the Girls of Enghelab Street. They were arrested too. It is hard to convey now how much nerve their actions took. Women had been edging their scarves back for years, but taking one off in daylight, above the traffic, where the police could see their naked heads as clearly as everyone else, was something very few women had done in public, since the protests of 1979 and 1980.

Then, in September 2022, Mahsa Jina Amini died in custody of the morality police. Unlike the women on the boxes, she was not an activist: aged 22, a Kurdish woman visiting from Saqqez, a city 600 km west of Tehran, she’d been stopped because her loose headscarf was not covering enough of her hair. Her death brought thousands of people out on to the street in an outpouring of grief and anger. Women burned their headscarves. Cut their hair in front of cameras. Their protests spawned the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, and continued for months. What began as a demand for justice for one woman became a challenge to the compulsory hijab, then to the system itself. The authorities responded with arrests, executions and a repression that has never really stopped. The funerals of the dead became protests in their turn.

W hat changed was that the morality police largely disappeared from the streets for months afterwards, with no announcement that the patrols had ended. Women who had grown up expecting to be stopped were not being stopped, and they knew why: the government had learned in 2022 what a single arrest could cost.

Azadeh, a woman from Tehran, tells me that, during the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, the city felt apocalyptic. After the US president Donald Trump posted that people in Tehran should get out of the city, they fled their homes, leaving everything behind, and the city emptied. Checkpoints multiplied as the government waited for an uprising that never came. But in the strange mood that settled on the city following the attacks, Azadeh noticed another change – a bargain that nobody signed: ‘The state began leaving people alone to live as they like, as long as they do not come out into the street about it.’

‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together’

What is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules that have governed daily life for decades. A few inches of visible hair used to be the whole argument, but it is no longer the point. Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. Enjoying this new freedom, they parade along Iranshahr (rather aptly, the street takes its name from the old Persian word for the land of the Iranians), where shops that used to sell manteaus and headscarves have switched to blouses and T-shirts.

A young woman whom I’ll call Mina puts the shift in blunter terms. ‘It isn’t optional anymore,’ she said. ‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together.’ She does not wear a headscarf anymore, and nor does anyone she goes out with. On the streets where people go to be seen, she tells me, hardly anyone does. In Tehran, those who can afford it wear the latest designer clothing. But in small Iranian towns, local workshops turn out such good copies of the latest Parisian and New York trends that anyone can now dress head to toe in ‘Chanel’, whatever their class.

Sima, also from Tehran, says that: ‘Among the women who dress freely there is a kind of solidarity. Nobody talks about it, but everyone feels it.’ Recalling the first time she removed her headscarf, Sima says: ‘I felt bald … I thought everyone was looking at me, and I kept checking.’ She was frightened, she told me, so she kept a headscarf in her bag ready to whip out if anything should happen. It took a while for the feeling to pass. Each time she went out, she saw more women without headscarves and that gave her heart. She knew that she was not alone.

T he easy read on these developments, especially outside Iran, is that this is defiance: using clothing as a weapon against the state. The framing is not entirely wrong, but it misses most of what is happening on the street, and the people living it do not describe what they are up to in this way. When I asked Mina if getting dressed felt like a political act, she paused, then said no. ‘When I dress up, it’s only for myself,’ she told me. ‘I’m not doing some political act.’ So what is happening on Iranshahr?

The Iranian sociologist Asef Bayat has spent years asking how ordinary people can change their societies in the absence of formal organisations or conventional political movements. In Life as Politics: How Ordinary People Change the Middle East (2010), he argues that they do it less by protesting than by simply living as they wish to, and in enough numbers and for long enough that the rules have to bend around them. Bayat’s name for what Sima, Mina and Azadeh are describing is ‘the art of presence’. It denotes ‘the courage and creativity to assert collective will in spite of all odds, to circumvent constraints, utilising what is available and discovering new spaces within which to make oneself heard, seen, felt, and realised.’ It is a form of soft power.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Optimism is a rare sight in this day and age — which is why scholar Arlene Dávila’s unabashed excitement about Latinx art right now is so invigorating. These artists draw from vernacular traditions, community histories, family memories, and more to reframe the narrative, despite facing a barrage of attacks in recent years. “The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry,” she writes in an opinion piece today. “Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.”

Read on for a pulse on the rest of the art world, from novelist Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, to Martin Puryear’s quietly revolutionary sculptures, to a new film reevaluating Frida Kahlo’s legacy and commodification. And it wouldn’t be the art world without some auction drama. Today, heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting it valued at $180 million, alleging that the work was sold under duress during World War II. Meanwhile, at Christie’s, a Willem de Kooning painting that entered the Whitney’s collection just a few years ago is headed under the hammer as Marquee Week kicks off in NYC.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries

Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. | Arlene Dávila

“Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere

Opening November 21 at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York, this exhibition includes masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries.

  • Many arts and culture organizations are bracing for what could be a series of politically targeted attacks from the Trump administration after reports that the White House is considering an executive order that would strip nonprofits deemed to have alleged “terrorist ties” of their tax-exempt status.
  • Heirs of a prominent Jewish publishing family call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a rare Vincent van Gogh painting highlighted in the marquee auction sales in New York City this week, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe.

Martin Puryear’s Liberatory Violence

Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“La ciudad es más que la gente.” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to Invasión’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters Adolfo Bioy Casares. Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled Borges) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own ficciones, it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that Invasión was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in one version with optional English and French subtitles, and another, higher resolution version with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding foley work and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, Nouvelle Vague, political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about Invasión, there is no one answer.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Given recent history, the prospect of hundreds of young men meeting on Facebook, then traveling from around the country to a central U.S. location might sound like reasonable cause for alarm. Yet a convention fitting that description had nothing to do with political violence but, rather, a celebration and appreciation of the name “Josh” (full disclosure: this writer did not attend). The gathering of the Joshes in April 2021 in Nebraska could not have been more peaceful, including its finishing battle royale, conducted with pool noodles.

The Joshes had no concern for proper pool-noodle-wielding technique, if there is such a thing. But groups of people who gather around the country to stage medieval-style battles in live-action role playing (LARP) games with weapons both real and fake might benefit from pointers.

So, too, might those who choreograph sword fights on stage and screen. Where can serious historical re-creators learn how to wield a real blade in historically accurate combat? One resource can be found at Wiktenauer, a wiki devoted to collecting “all of the primary and secondary source literature that makes up the text of historical European Martial arts (HEMA) research.”

The Fior di Battaglia (“Flower of Battle”)—an Italian fencing manual by Fiore de’i Liberi dating from circa 1404—offers richly- and copiously-illustrated demonstrations of medieval Italian longsword fighting techniques. In the original manuscript, seen here and at The Getty, “the illustrations are inked sketches with gold leafing on the crowns and garters,” notes the Wiktenauer entry. They dominate the text, which “takes the form of descriptive paragraphs set in poor Italian verse, which are nevertheless fairly clear and informative.” So clear, indeed, the brooding young men of Akademia Szermierzy—a Polish group that recreates medieval sword-fighting techniques—can more than convincingly mimic the moves in the video at the top.

Once they get going, after some requisite pre-fight rigmarole, it’s impressive stuff, maybe already familiar to modern fencers and certain members of the Society for Creative Anachronism, the LARP-ing organization of amateurs recreating everything from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. But for those who think all live-action role-playing is the equivalent of the Battle of the Joshes (or off-brand Nazis running through the streets in homemade armor), the sheer ballet of historical sword-fighting may come as a surprise — and maybe inspire a few more people to pull on the doublet and hose. See more medieval sword-fighting recreations from Akademia Szermierzy here, and the full text of the Fior di Battaglia here.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2021.

items.title: New “Central Dogma of Aging” Highlights the Complexity of Getting Older
items.author: Jake Currie
items.summary: Imbalances pile up as we age The post New “Central Dogma of Aging” Highlights the Complexity of Getting Older appeared first on Nautilus .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Originally proposed by Francis Crick (of Watson and Crick) in 1958, the central dogma of molecular biology states that information flows from DNA to RNA to protein. Now, in a new study published in Innovation Life , experts on aging have proposed a new central dogma of aging.

For fans of the original central dogma, this new framework has plenty to love. It builds on the trusty DNA → RNA → protein scaffold and adds a fourth layer: metabolites. These small molecules are the end products and intermediaries of the cellular processes that keep you alive, like glucose, ATP, pyruvic acid, and many, many, many more. All four are governed by three processes: anabolism (building up), modification, and catabolism (breaking down).

Unlike the traditional central dogma, information within this model flows in multiple directions and problems in one layer can affect the others. As we get older, this interdependent network deteriorates. Take damaged DNA, for example. Faulty genetic material can lead to RNA transcriptional errors, activate inflammation pathways, lead to faulty proteins that occupy cellular recycling processes and throw a wrench into metabolism, etc. Metabolites can then feedback on genetic control via epigenetics. When the four-layer system slips out of balance over time, problems stack up.

Of course, no one ages in a vacuum. So surrounding the four layers is the exposome—the environmental factors that influence the system. These factors can be anything from oxygen and hormones on a micro level to diet, sleep, and pollution on a macro level.

You may be curious why we don’t already have a model for understanding aging, and the truth is we do. The Hallmarks of Aging catalogs a dozen changes that occur in our bodies as we age, like stem cell exhaustion, poorer nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, and more.

According to the team, this new framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of aging and “a novel lens” for “combating aging and age-related decline,” as they write. The researchers characterize the Hallmarks as a kind of parallel checklist that focuses more on DNA changes, largely omitting metabolites and RNA. Under this new model, aging is a complex series of conversations between every part of our cellular machinery.

While it’s still largely hypothetical, it could help explain why single-target aging interventions continue to miss the mark. The bottom line is: Our bodies are complicated machines, aging is a complicated process, and a holistic approach may be our best bet for understanding how to stay healthy into our golden years.

items.title: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
items.author: Rhea Nayyar
items.summary: “Yellow River” (1958) was deaccessioned and will be auctioned at Christie's just three years after it was gifted to the museum in 2023.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
Rhea Nayyar

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy. In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.

“I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a BBC interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”

“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum deaccessioned seven works, including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

items.title: Derelict Soviet Spacecraft? Dark Comet? What the Heck is 1998 KY26?
items.author: Jake Currie
items.summary: It’s behavior defies explanation The post Derelict Soviet Spacecraft? Dark Comet? What the Heck is 1998 KY26? appeared first on Nautilus .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
An artist’s impression of Japan’s Hayabusa2 space mission touching down on the surface of the asteroid 1998 KY26. New observations with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (VLT) have revealed that 1998 KY26 is just 11 m wide, almost three times smaller than previously thought, and is spinning once every 5 minutes, which is much faster than expected. The image above shows an updated size comparison between the asteroid and spacecraft.

Hayabusa-2 is currently careening toward a rendezvous with the unknown. Launched in 2014, the Japanese spacecraft embarked on a mission to retrieve samples from asteroids and return them to Earth. It performed its duties admirably in 2018, spending a year and a half surveying the “rubble pile” asteroid Ryugu before swinging by its home planet to drop off the goods. Inside the sample return canister were traces of organic compounds from the dawn of the solar system.

Now its mission has been extended until at least 2031, when it should reach its next target: the smaller, speedier, more mysterious 1998 KY26. This peculiar celestial object has puzzled astronomers since its discovery nearly 30 years ago. It’s relatively tiny—not much bigger than Hayabusa-2 itself and roughly 1/100th the diameter of Ryugu—and it rotates at a brisk clip of once every 5.35 minutes.

Read more: “ Nine Rebel Astronomy Theories That Went Dark ”

But the weirdest thing about 1998 KY26 is its acceleration. Instead of smoothly zipping around the sun like a normal asteroid it tends to lurch perpendicular to its orbit in unpredictable ways. This odd behavior led Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and colleagues to argue it wasn’t an asteroid at all, but the derelict Soviet space probe Phobos 1 (the paper, published earlier this year, hasn’t been peer reviewed).

Of course, there are other explanations for this kind of activity. For example, it’s possible 1998 KY26 is a “dark comet.” Comets get their magnificent tails from the sun heating icy particles that jet out into space. Dark comets, on the other hand, are asteroids that keep their icy material hidden beneath the surface. They can act like comets, but without the telltale tail.

Unfortunately, a new study published in the journal Icarus is throwing cold water on the dark asteroid theory—or rather, warm regolith. Per an analysis of 1998 KY26 conducted by aerospace engineers from the Georgia Institute of Technology, the object is much too warm to harbor any ice. “Our temperature model results indicate that the water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice, refining the understanding of the asteroid’s composition,” the researchers wrote. If 1998 KY26 ever had secret pockets of frozen water, they would have been depleted long ago.

We still don’t know for sure, but not knowing is the first step on the path toward knowing. While we speculate back on Earth, mark your calendars for July 2031—that’s when Hayabusa-2 makes contact.

Lead Image: ESO/M. Kornmesser. Asteroid: T. Santana-Ros et al; Hayabusa2 model: SuperTKG / Wikimedia Commons

items.title: The Bloomsbury Group's Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant Tangled Their Art and Lives Together for Decades. A Final Sketch of Bell on Her Deathbed Just Resurfaced After 60 Years
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The two artists had a thoroughly complicated relationship—and a daughter—but never ceased to paint and draw each other. The new discovery points to an artistic bond that continued through health and sickness

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Christian Thorsberg
Vanessa Bell

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The lives of artists Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell —collaborators, companions and sometimes lovers—were deeply intertwined both on canvases and in private quarters.

The pair were central figures in the Bloomsbury Group , a circle of artists and intellectuals active in early 20th-century Britain who radically, and often controversially, challenged contemporary creative and social norms. These included public sentiments on philosophy, sexuality and mental illness. The group featured, among others, the economist John Maynard Keynes , as well as the writers E. M. Forster and Virginia Woolf , Bell’s biological sister.

Grant and Bell were often the subjects of each other’s work. Among their most well-known collaborations is one of Grant’s first and most extravagant depictions of Bell, a full-length portrait painted in 1915.

But this summer, while preparing for “ Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury ,” an exhibition that opened this week at Tate Britain, scholars discovered an intimate, previously unknown work that sheds new light on the end of Grant and Bell’s relationship.

Hidden for some 60 years among private family papers, the newly recovered drawing is thought to be Grant’s final depiction of Bell. Created in an uncharacteristically simple style—soft monochrome pencil and biro on paper—the piece shows an ailing Bell with her eyes closed, head resting on a pillow, from the perspective of an artist who likely was sitting at her bedside. In the bottom right-hand corner, Grant dated the piece April 14, 1961—one week after Bell succumbed to an illness at the age of 81, and two days after her burial.

“I found this drawing deeply moving when I first saw it. We know Duncan’s drawings of Vanessa so intimately, made over the course of their long friendship, that the discovery of a previously unknown work is remarkable in itself,” Nathaniel Hepburn , director of Charleston , the pair’s former home and studio in East Sussex , says in a statement . “But there is something incredibly poignant about imagining Duncan sitting beside Vanessa, drawing her after her death.”

The drawing is considered an emotional bookend to the pair’s decades-long relationship. In a 1937 letter to her son, Bell described Grant as “so incredibly full of charm, his genius as an artist seems to overflow so into his life and character & he is so amusing too and odd and unaccountable that lots of people I think don’t see clearly what to me is really his most adorable quality—his honesty…”

Scholars believe that Grant may have erred slightly, perhaps affected by grief, in his dating of the drawing.

“What seems very likely here is that Duncan knew this drawing had been made around Vanessa’s death and later added a date from memory,” Darren Clarke , head of collections and research at Charleston, says in the statement. “He got remarkably close, but apparently not quite close enough. Everything about the drawing itself—its viewpoint, its intimacy and its extraordinary economy—suggests someone sitting quietly beside Vanessa’s bed and drawing the face he had known for half a century.”

Though it won’t feature in the new Tate show, the drawing will enter into a permanent collection at Charleston as part of the institution’s “ 50 for 50 ” campaign, which seeks to secure 50 more works by prominent Bloomsbury Group figures by 2030. In May 2027, after the completion of renovations, it will be put on display for the very first time.

Bell had a daughter, Angelica , with Grant in 1918. Bell raised Angelica as the daughter of Clive Bell , her husband, and did not reveal Angelica’s true father until she turned 18.

At the Tate exhibition, which opened last week and runs through April, some 300 portraits, still lives, landscape paintings and other works guide visitors through the intertwined lives of Grant and Bell, as well as their involvement with the Bloomsbury Group.

“It’s so fascinating to see the ways they differ,” Thomas Kennedy, curator of Modern British art at Tate Britain, tells the Art Newspaper ’s Andrew Pulver. “We should recognize their individual accomplishments of course, but also the works they made together and how they influenced each other.”

“ Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury ” is on view at Tate Britain in London until April 11, 2027.

Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi
Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism, a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.

Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two new books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality

“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallergic about her first book, “Ten Lives.” | Lakshmi Rivera Amin

Fall 2026 Art and Architecture Books from Yale University Press

The Bayeux tapestry, a new biography of Edward Hopper, The Met’s exhibition catalogue on Krasner and Pollock, what architecture is, and more

The Jewish Sisters in Renoir’s “Pink and Blue”

Author Catherine Ostler follows the lives of the two cherubic girls, whose rarefied lives in an elite, artistic French family would be toppled by the horrors of the Holocaust. | Eurídice Arratia

The Art World’s Neoliberal Capture

In “The Battleground of Art,” curator and activist Marco Baravalle dissects the art establishment’s co-optation of radical politics and uplifts the stories of collectives that resist it. | Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain

Guadalupe Rosales’s Portable Archive of East LA

In two new books, the artist weaves her archive of photos, ephemera, and flyers into the story of ’90s Chicanx youth culture, tracing both a personal and collective coming-of-age. | Carolina A. Miranda

It’s Time to Talk About Classism in the Art World

In his memoiristic new book, photographer Mark Alice Durant weaves his personal experiences into a larger rebuke of the economic inequality that governs the art world. | Melissa Holbrook Pierson

New Art Books from the Quarto Group

From art history to instruction, Quarto publishes visually-rich books for artists of all mediums and skill levels.

A review of an ancient Chinese ink painting takes an art critic on a journey through his own past. | Will Heinrich

  • M. John Harrison won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, and readers and literary critics are split. Some are thrilled to see a science fiction title nab the award, a first in its nearly six-decade history. But the shortlist included a few undeniable favorites, like Jamaican novelist Marlon James’s The Disappearers, and the prize committee has a tendency to favor White, male authors (shocker!). I plan to read both and make up my mind after; let me know your thoughts in the meantime.
  • Natalie Renganeschi is joining the Women’s Studio Workshop, a center for printmaking, bookbinding, and other paper-related arts, as executive director.
  • After five years, Michelle T. Boone is retiring from her post as president and CEO of the Poetry Foundation.
  • A Mario Vargas Llosa biography that was in the works for 13 years got dropped by Penguin for being what it deemed too critical of the Peruvian author.
  • A Truman Capote estate auction has a few odd items up for grabs, namely the ashes of his dog Maggie. The wonders of auction houses never cease.
  • Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, whose memoir was nominated for a National Book Award, has a must-read essay out about the US’s denial of the visitor visa he requested to attend the ceremony in New York City this Wednesday. [New Yorker]
  • If you’ve ever wanted to create a time capsule, Ashley Stimpson has some thoughts. She writes about the history of the practice, the slim odds that a time capsule will ever be found, and why you should make one anyway. [Longreads]
  • During her pregnancy, filmmaker Siraad Dirshe found solace in books like Sasha Bonét’s The Waterbearers, a reminder of the need to archive, narrate, and preserve stories of Black motherhood. [Literary Hub]

Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
As I rejoin the queue for the Valeria Luiselli book that expired on my Kindle — the Brooklyn Public Library doesn’t play about digital loans — I’ve added a romance novel to my rotation: Ali Hazelwood’s The Love Hypothesis (2021). It’s predictable, it’s corny, and it’s just STEM enough to make me feel like I’m learning something about scientific research funding and early-detection cancer biomarkers. Truly the perfect holiday-season read.

items.title: What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind
items.author: Stephanie Wambugu
items.summary: "Requiem" is a fitting self-elegy for the painter, precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
What Mary Lovelace O
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful. 

The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them.

The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows. 

Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous through the hands of a master craftsman. 

During this formative and fruitful period between the 1970s and 1990s, when her visual language and iconoclastic artistic sensibility crystallized, O’Neal was also coming into her own as an artist. She was a groundbreaking student, becoming the first Black woman to receive an MFA from Columbia University in 1969, and in 1985, she became the first African American professor to receive tenure in UC Berkeley’s Department of Art Practice. 

The back room offers a rich sketch of the painter’s life as it intersected with both world history and art history. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1942, Jim Crow was fully in place in the American South during the artist’s childhood.  She attended Howard University in 1960 alongside David Driskell and Lois Mailou Jones, dated the activist Stokely Carmichael, and was an activist in her own right. 

The archival materials reveal the cultural and political concerns of O’Neal’s time. It’s all the more remarkable that she navigated these constraints while retaining the verve and genuine, delightful strangeness these paintings must have necessitated. “Untitled” (n.d.) gets at the humor and irreverence of O’Neal’s style. An Uncle Sam-like figure, half-covered in chalky white paint, evokes a satirical Ralph Bakshi cartoon, with many identifying features erased. It has a winking quality. Though political in nature, it foregrounds O’Neal’s formal concerns, which circle mainly around the possibilities of certain pigments (like the enveloping darkness of lampblack contrasted with punchy neons) and the permeable boundary between abstraction and figuration. It is this formal rigor that made O’Neal trailblazing in more ways than one –– both as a Black American shattering institutional barriers and as a woman painter making important interventions into the inherited, lionized artistic movements of the Color Field, Abstract Expressionism, and Minimalism. 

“Race Woman Series #7” (1992–93) dramatizes the tension between the structural or compositional and the political, suggesting that it was an enduring preoccupation for the artist. A dazed face vaguely springs up from a prominent green being, which could just be read as an indecipherable scrawl, while a white specter at the top of the canvas drips over it. O’Neal’s use of color is frenetic and instinctive, resulting in a painting that is too varied to slot into a clear interpretation. Like the Klannish chiaroscuro of Norman Lewis’ “Alabama” (1960), the legibility of “Race Woman Series #7” relies on the light its instructive title sheds on it. 

But unlike Lewis, when we search for correlation between O’Neal’s caption and the canvas, we are pulled deeper into her self-reflexive, numinous and unrepeatable idiom, which makes its own intuitive sense and, anyway, seeks to go beyond sense-making into the terrain of near-mystical experience. 

Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem continues at Boesky Gallery (509 West 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan) through December 19. The exhibition is organized by the gallery.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
With no cure for Alzheimer’s on the horizon, and our best treatments only slowing the progression of the disease, there’s been an intense effort to find earlier means of detection. Now, a new study published in Neuroimage Reports is offering hope of diagnosis even before cognitive symptoms become noticeable.   

A team of biomedical imaging specialists, pathologists, and neuroscientists from Johns Hopkins University studied how the brains of older adults changed over time by analyzing hundreds of MRI scans and PET scans. They relied on longitudinal data from two different studies (the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study) that included people from across the Alzheimer’s spectrum, from cognitively healthy to full-blown dementia.

Read more: “How the Brain’s Failing Trash Compactor Can Contribute to Alzheimer’s Disease”
