items.title: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Two nests were spotted in September, and authorities moved the eggs to an aquarium to protect them from an incoming tropical storm. Over the weekend, dozens of hatchlings emerged and have now been released on the same beaches where they were found

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In September, authorities in California were baffled to find two sea turtle nests on their beaches—the first natural ones ever confirmed on the United States’ West Coast. Now, dozens of the eggs have hatched. Experts released the baby olive ridley turtles over the weekend, allowing the tiny creatures to begin their perilous journeys to adulthood.

The two nests were identified on Seal Beach and Huntington Beach in Orange County. Because a tropical storm was coming soon after the nests were found, biologists moved the more than 200 eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific. The Ping-Pong ball-size spheres stayed in closed incubators under sand in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, simulating their ideal natural conditions.

Aquarium staff first saw signs of hatching activity on November 12, when they noticed changes in the surface of the sand in the incubation container with the Seal Beach eggs, said Lance Adams , the aquarium’s veterinarian, during a press conference on November 14. The team spotted a depression and some cracks in the sand, indicating something was happening beneath it. The first turtle emerged the following day at around 7:15 p.m. Pacific time. Around two hours later, more of the baby turtles from the Seal Beach nest started popping out, resulting in 54 squirming critters.

“It kind of went from looking like very smooth beach sand to looking like an eruption of baby sea turtles,” Adams explained. It “was really exciting and very, very cute.” As of the press conference date, 50 eggs from the nest had not hatched. Experts do not know whether they’re viable, but they will continue monitoring the makeshift home.

The Seal Beach hatchlings were released in the same location where their nest had been, very early on Saturday morning, before the sun had risen, according to a social media post . That’s because baby turtles use moonlight to navigate toward the ocean. After reaching the water, hatchlings experience a “frenzy period” in which they swim continuously for 24 to 48 hours, according to the post. The energetic outburst is justified; experts estimate that only one in 1,000 olive ridley turtle hatchlings survive to adulthood, according to a statement .

The Huntington Beach eggs weren’t too far behind, with many hatchlings emerging shortly after the Seal Beach eggs. They were returned to Huntington Beach on Sunday, also under the cover of darkness during the wee morning hours. All the released hatchlings made it to the water, according to the statement.

Olive ridley turtles are among the smallest sea turtles in the world, growing to approximately two feet long and weighing between 70 to 100 pounds.

Olive ridleys are some of the most abundant and widespread sea turtles in the world. Unfortunately, all their populations are considered threatened or endangered. The species is mostly found in the tropical regions of the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, and experts still don’t know why or how these nests ended up in the contiguous United States.

“There’s never been a recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on a California beach,” Jeff Flocken , president and CEO of the Aquarium of the Pacific, told SFGate ’s Olivia Harden in September. “Typically, the most north we know of any olive ridley or any sea turtle that nests are in Mexico, so this is quite a bit farther north for them.”

Around that time, Justin Viezbicke , California stranding coordinator for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, told the Guardian ’s Lois Beckett that the mother turtles may have lost their way because of a hurricane. The ongoing “super” El Niño in the Pacific Ocean, which is affecting water temperatures, currents and weather, may also have helped push them to California.

However, biologist Jonathan Snyder , of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, has a more hopeful outlook. “I think the warm waters along the coast are certainly part of the story, but I think there’s another really important part of the story,” he said during the press conference.

Decades of sea turtle conservation efforts have “really moved the needle” for olive ridleys, he noted. “Their populations have increased substantially throughout the portions of the range, and it’s the reason that there are these sea turtles along our coast that could take advantage of these unique environmental conditions.”

In fact, authorities found a third nest farther north in California’s Ventura County on November 1, but it was destroyed by high tides, Snyder tells the Los Angeles Times ’ Corinne Purtill. Regardless, experts still aren’t sure whether the recent nests will continue to represent an unusual event or they are the start of a new normal.

Margherita Bassi is a freelance journalist and trilingual storyteller. Her work has appeared in publications including BBC Travel, Discover magazine, Live Science , Atlas Obscura and Hidden Compass .

items.title: A French Court Annuls the $1.6 Million Sale of This Camille Pissarro Painting, Allegedly Looted During World War II
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Seven descendants of Jewish banker Salomon Flavian challenged a 2024 auction sale brokered without their knowledge, prompting a court to demand the painting's restitution and the revelation of the anonymous buyer's identity

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In 1941, German forces in occupied Paris looted a Jewish banker’s collection of impressionist artworks. Now, more than eight decades later, a French court has stepped in to demand the return of one allegedly looted painting to the descendants of its owner.

A 1902 landscape by Camille Pissarro titled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée ( Fishing Dock and Duquesne Basin, Dieppe, Sunny Afternoon ) was auctioned by Sotheby’s London on June 25, 2024, to an anonymous buyer for roughly $1.6 million. On November 5, the Paris Judicial Court annulled that sale and ordered Sotheby’s to “disclose the full identity of the buyer of the work” within two months or pay a $1,115 fine for every additional day it fails to do so, CNN’s Lianne Kolirin reports.

Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in history , seizing more than 650,000 artworks across Europe—some 20 percent of the continent’s art—including from Jewish families, collectors and museums.

Salomon Flavian, a Jewish banker of French and Romanian heritage, purchased Pissarro’s view of the Normandy port town of Dieppe at the Hôtel Drouot auction house in Paris in March 1935, according to the Sotheby’s listing .

When war erupted in September 1939, Flavian placed the canvas and dozens of other works into the care of the Westminster Foreign Bank in Paris. In 1941, German forces seized his collection. Although Flavian survived the war and recovered some pieces, the Pissarro remained missing and was listed in France’s official register of looted property.

Nearly eight decades later, the painting resurfaced at Sotheby’s London with a note stating that it was “offered for sale pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian.” That settlement had been brokered by the Mondex Corporation , a Toronto-based firm specializing in recovering Nazi-looted art.

At a hearing in this fall, seven descendants of Flavian told the court that two relatives had signed the deal without consulting the rest of the family. The descendants claimed they had only found out about the sale months later, when Mondex sent a letter explaining that it had accepted in their name a “relatively modest” 8 percent share of the net sale price “in exchange for their cooperation,” while the two heirs who signed the contract received a 16 percent commission, the Art Newspaper ’s Vincent Noce reported in September.

At the hearing, Sotheby’s and Mondex presented research claiming that Flavian had parted with the painting before the war, pointing to a 1939 Pissarro catalogue raisonné by Paris dealer Paul Rosenberg that listed British artist and collector Edward Le Bas as the owner. Sotheby’s auction provenance similarly traced the canvas from Flavian to Rosenberg by 1937 and to Le Bas by 1939. It then eventually passed through several American collections, including David Rockefeller’s, and a 1985 sale at Sotheby’s New York.

Earlier this month, the Paris court rejected that timeline, finding “no direct and convincing evidence” of prewar sales to Rosenberg or Le Bas, according to the Art Newspaper . Instead, the court concluded that the family presented “a set of precise, serious and concurring elements demonstrating that Pissarro’s work was indeed looted during” the war.

The court ordered “the restitution of the work, wherever and in whoever’s possession it may be, to the descendants of Salomon Flavian,” the London Times ’ David Chazan reports.

“It is a very important ruling, which opens the way to a restitution that the Flavian family has demanded since the war,” Corinne Hershkovitch, the claimants’ lawyer, tells the Art Newspaper .

In May, the Musée d’Orsay in Paris opened a new permanent exhibition titled “ Who Owns These Works? ” It showcases 13 artworks that may have been looted or sold under suspicious circumstances during World War II with the hope that public exposure may help locate the rightful owners.

Mondex, which was ordered to pay $11,000 to the heirs, plans to challenge the verdict. Mondex founder James Palmer tells ARTnews ’ Brian Boucher that an appeal will be filed “forthwith.” He adds: “We are confident that when the vast amount of complex provenance research evidence is properly understood and considered that the court of appeal will reach a different conclusion.”

Because the French judgment applies immediately despite any appeal, the legal battle now shifts toward enforcing the order across the English Channel. Hershkovitch, however, tells the Times that cross-border enforcement between France and England is “a fairly simple procedure.” She adds: “Sotheby’s will have to find a solution very quickly because their reputation is at stake.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
From an early mishmash of chaotic lines and misspelled words to the loose lilt of a signature scribbled for decades, “Paper Trail” is a moving animation that shows the evolution of a young mind and what we can glean from a life through notes and lists. The latest project by Don Hertzfeldt, the short film follows the protagonist Steven Richardson as he makes his first marks, learns to write his name, doodles, and later completes the perfunctory math problems of elementary school. We witness his cursive lessons and adolescent love letters to a girl named Lindsey before observing grocery lists and remnants of his professional life.

Based in Austin, Texas, Hertzfeldt is known for his poetic animations that harness the indelible intimacy of hand-drawn scenes. “Paper Trail” has been on the festival circuit where it’s garnered top honors at Annecy, Sundance, SXSW, and many others. The film is available for streaming for a limited-timed on Vimeo, along with more of Hertzfeldt’s work.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Come November and December, northerly climes brace for dropping temperatures and the first snow. Winter may not be everyone’s favorite, and it’s easy to dwell on gray days and leafless trees. Fortunately, when the sun shines, the cold months can also reveal abundant life and beauty, and many woodland denizens thrive during this time of the year. It’s a side of the season that photographer Roeselien Raimond expresses in her series Zen & The Art of Winter Foxes.

Raimond documents serene vulpine creatures in moments of repose amid peaceful, snowy surrounds. “The images are part of a personal project about the unexpected connection between nature, photography and inner peace,” the artist tells Colossal. “The idea originated from an encounter with a vixen during a snowstorm, when I found myself feeling completely at ease despite the freezing conditions.”

Meeting the reclusive animal spurred an ongoing series and exploration of the Zen paradox of desire, in which the search for something can make it more difficult to find. Raimond taps into nature’s powerful lesson that quietude and mindfulness can help us to recharge, just like the foxes’ natural inclination to rest, reflect, and simply soak up some rays. See more on Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Conjure an image of a basket in your mind. Is it made of straw, or perhaps sweetgrass or willow? Does it have a handle? Was it made by hand, and what could it hold? At Mindy Solomon Gallery, a forthcoming exhibition titled Interwoven: Basketry As Expanded Practice challenges our perception of both object and craft.

Curated by Dee Clements, the exhibition considers the way basketmaking techniques are far from limited to the splinted white ash trug we might carry out to the garden or the simple vessel that holds recipes in the kitchen. This vibrant survey “breaks craft tradition,” Clements says, positioning the practice as an art form. The show asks “what happens when basketry is understood not as a fixed category of craft, but as an open-ended artistic language?”

The artists in Interwoven use a range of materials, from ceramic and steel to cotton and paper. Salvador Dominguez’s vibrant pipe cleaner vessels are complemented by wall works like Eric Gushee’s intricately interlaced wire sculptures and Miguel Arzabe’s woven, deconstructed paintings.

Viewers will find further explorations by artists like Dienke Dekker and José Santiago Pérez, who work with unexpected materials like paper and emergency blankets, respectively. And Colossal readers might also recognize work by Xanthe Somers and Sonia Barrett, among the nearly two dozen participating artists.

Interwoven opens on November 29 and continues through January 9 in Miami. See more on the gallery’s Instagram.

The 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera is mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope on Cerro Tololo near La Serena, Chile.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/ DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

J oshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to plan a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then, in early 1998, two teams of researchers announced that exploding stars called supernovas seemed to be racing away from Earth under the influence of an unidentified, omnipresent repellent force. The observations implied the existence of exactly the sort of missing energy that Frieman and his colleagues planned to talk about.

“Suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop,” including reporters with TV cameras, said Frieman, who was then at the University of Chicago. It was “kind of a circus.”

Within a few years, cosmologists had arrived at a whole new view of reality. The missing energy, given the name “dark energy” for its invisible nature, was pushing galaxies apart. The energy seemed embedded in space itself. It made up roughly two-thirds of creation (with matter — visible and dark — making up the remainder). Frieman embarked on what would become a two-decade mission to learn about dark energy by watching how it influences all that we can see: the Dark Energy Survey (DES).

Now that project has come to a close. In May 2026, DES shared findings based on its full dataset of thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies spanning billions of years of cosmic history. Those findings, in combination with data gathered by a different project, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), suggest that our understanding of what the universe is made of — the venerable “standard model” of cosmology — is not complete. “There appear to be cracks in that model,” said Simone Ferraro , a cosmologist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “There’s something that doesn’t fit.”

Joshua Frieman, a physicist now at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, co-founded the Dark Energy Survey to examine the accelerating expansion of the universe.

Cosmologists can’t yet say what that something is. What they can say is that after 20 years of stability, their field is returning to a state of confusion. “It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited,” Ferraro said.

Experimental cosmology is a piecemeal endeavor. It’s a bit like trying to reconstruct a person’s life from a dossier of data about them: report cards, utility bills, cholesterol tests, and so on. You come up with a story that weaves all the data together, go find new data, and use it to refine the story. Frieman and other cosmologists started to speculate about a missing form of energy in the mid-1990s because the story they were telling didn’t seem quite right.

In previous decades, they had peered at the sky and inferred roughly how much stuff was out there. They saw a smattering of galaxies lighting up the void — visible matter. Based on how fast the galaxies were spinning, astronomers deduced that a preponderance of invisible matter must surround each bright speck, holding it together — dark matter.

It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited.

The rate at which these galaxies were receding from view implied that the universe had been expanding for some 8 billion to 13 billion years. It looked as if there was just enough matter (dark and visible combined) to tug gravitationally on the universe and continuously slow this expansion without ever bringing it to a full halt.

But new observations started to clash with this accounting. Astronomers spotted stars, for instance, that seemed to be older than the universe. While trying to understand these and other anomalies, cosmologists noticed that it helped to add a new type of energy to their models.

items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: The 19th-century craftsman extolled the universal right to beauty. The problem was that his handmade items were necessarily expensive

Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Amy Crawford
Flora, designed by William Morris and Edward Coley Burne-Jones, made by William Knight, William Sleath and John Martin for Morris & Company,

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Born into a wealthy English family, William Morris (1834-1896) grew up in the countryside, honing a love for nature that found expression in fabric and wallpaper he designed for his successful firm, Morris & Company. An activist as well as an artist and businessman, he loathed the inequity of Victorian society and the soullessness of the industrial age, coming to embrace revolutionary socialism.

But while he believed in a universal right to beauty, his own careful craftsmanship held a certain contradiction, says Amy George, curator of a retrospective of Morris’ original designs opening this month at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England. “Anything handmade is expensive,” she notes. “And it should be expensive, because of the labor that goes into it.”

Perhaps ironically, in recent years capitalism has made Morris’ work more accessible, as it has appeared on products from mass-market brands like H&M and Williams Sonoma. In a way, it seems, his goal of art for all may finally have been realized.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

Amy Crawford is a Michigan-based freelance journalist writing about cities, science, the environment, art and education. A longtime Smithsonian contributor, her work also appears in CityLab and the Boston Globe .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In Fort Worth, Texas, a massive, dilapidated building serves as an ever-present symbol of racial violence and segregation to those who know its history. Constructed in the 1920s, the structure, initially known as Klavern No 101 , was briefly the auditorium and headquarters of Fort Worth’s Ku Klux Klan chapter. It stood between downtown and the North Side, where migrants and communities of colour had settled, so many residents had to pass it on their way to work. In this short documentary, the director Chris Neighbors, a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, brings together scholars, community members and those directly involved in redesigning the space to reflect on its past and the thinking behind its transformation into an arts and community centre. Filmed inside the building itself, their conversations consider a question that extends far beyond Fort Worth: how do we preserve difficult histories without preserving the values they once stood for?

items.author: Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene
items.summary: Civilisation wasn’t made possible by grain, but by transportation – and the conquest it enabled, from the steppe to the sea - by Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A horse rider at the market place in Urga (now Ulaanbaatar), Mongolia, photographed by Stéphane Passet in July 1913. Courtesy the Musée Albert-Kahn, France

is professor of history and anthropology at the National University of Mongolia. He is also a visiting scholar with the Mongolia and Inner Asia Studies Unit (MIASU) at the University of Cambridge, UK. He is the author of The Taiji Government and the Rise of the Warrior State: The Formation of the Qing Imperial Constitution (2022) and The Nomadic Leviathan: A Critique of the Sinocentric Paradigm (2023).

Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age.

No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest.

As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state.

Contemporary live marine traffic map available at marinetraffic.com

W hoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.

Conquering the world on horseback is easy, as the saying goes. On land, equids – donkeys and horses – forged states and civilisations, while the llama did the same for the Inkas. Ur’s kunga chariots project the military might of Mesopotamian cities, and the Abydos donkeys demonstrate their vital role in early Egyptian kingship. By the end of the 3rd millennium BCE, Central Eurasian nomads were entombing entire horse chariots – the high-tech, high-value war machines of their time – to honour their kings in Sintashta. Horse chariots later symbolised the power of the Shang and the Zhou; the latter deployed 4,000 chariots to overwhelm the former in 1046 BCE.

Building a state does not require grain, but does demand extrahuman transportation

‘The rider appears on the stage of history like a new breed of man’ – a centaur, as the German sociologist Alexander Rüstow put it in the 1950s. Eurasian nomads had long bred their mounts into the modern domestic horse, paving the way for an age of empires that would fundamentally reshape the world. Horses dominated human history for nearly four millennia. Even for maritime powers, horses remained key to conquest; from Carthage to the British, all relied on horses for inland expansion. Francisco Pizarro’s conquest of the Inkas is a prime illustration of the power of horses against an essentially pedestrian empire built on llama transportation. Horses also enabled the Comanche in North America to forge their empire and compete with European powers for nearly a century.

Comanche warriors, photographed in 1892. Courtesy Wikipedia

The Comanche Empire? Did they actually have grain to build a state? No, they had no grain – nor any agriculture, for that matter. Horse husbandry and bison hunting sustained their livelihood. In fact, all the Eurasian steppe powers – including the Mongols – relied on pastoralism. What they enjoyed most was an abundance of extrahuman transportation; what they lacked most was agricultural produce. Ultimately, building a state does not require grain, but it does demand extrahuman transportation.

Look at the political geography of the Roman and Mongol empires: the Romans could reach where ships could reach, and the Mongols could reach where horses could reach. The same is true of European colonial empires; it all comes down to the power of extrahuman transportation. Donkeys, horses and all other herd animals are the creations of pastoralists. Extrahuman transportation made the state and civilisation possible; this places pastoralism at the origin of the state and civilisation, and the Eurasian steppe at the centre of human history.

The expansion of the Mongol Empire in the 13th century. Courtesy Wikipedia

items.cleanReaderHtml:
When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting explosion of public enthusiasm, the contemporary media initially struggled to find ways to describe the picture itself. “A cowboy movie set in space, that’s Star Wars,” pronounces the announcer in a TV news clip included in the new Nerdwriter video above. “It’s old-fashioned escapist entertainment, pure and simple.” That may have been all the Italian film industry needed to hear. The “spaghetti westerns” of the previous dozen years had proven that it could profitably master an American genre; surely it could do the same with a similar one.

Among the results, alas, one looks in vain for A Fistful of Dollars, or even a Navajo Joe. Nerdwriter creator Evan Puschak goes over various instances of shameless imitation that characterize the Italian Star Wars clones, but you don’t have to take his word for it; you can, in fact, find some of these movies on YouTube.

Luigi Cozzi’s StarCrash, for example, stars David Hasselhoff, The Spy Who Loved Me Bond girl Caroline Munro, and a Christopher Plummer putting in one of his most grandiosely villainous performances ever; Aldo Lado’s The Humanoid, an even more shameless knock-off, credits its director as “George B. Lewis.” Nor was Italy the only country cashing in on the Star Wars craze: Puschak also shows clips from the Japanese film Message From Space by no less an auteur than Battle Royale director Kinji Fukasaku.

Though many of these second-rate (at best) space operas made money, and some have even retained a certain charm nearly 50 years later, they all come up against the fundamental stinginess of the Cinecittà production model. “The truth is that you can’t imitate Star Wars with a low budget,” says Puschak. Despite all that’s been said about the myriad ways in which it taps into the power of universal myth, “the spectacle, the immersion induced by its groundbreaking special effects, was just as vital to the experience as the story and the characters.” Hard as it may be for today’s young viewers to believe, there was a time when moviegoers weren’t all that discriminating about the realism, or even the plausibility, of the visuals onscreen. After Star Wars, for better or for worse, they’d never overlook visible wires, unsteady lip-sync, or flat matte paintings so easily again.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his culture, becoming a vocal proponent of vegetarianism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thousands of his contemporaries found Tolstoy’s example deeply compelling, and several communes formed around his principles, to his dismay. “To speak of ‘Tolstoyism,’” he wrote, “to seek guidance, to inquire about my solution of questions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New Yorker, “people insisted on seeking guidance from him,” including a young Mahatma Gandhi, who struck up a lively correspondence with the writer and in 1910 founded a community called “Tolstoy Farm” near Johannesburg.

Though uneasy in the role of movement leader, the author of Anna Karenina invited such treatment by publishing dozens of philosophical and theological works, many of them in opposition to a contrary strain of religious and moral ideas developing in the late nineteenth century. Often called “muscular Christianity,” this trend responded to what many Victorians thought of as a crisis of masculinity by emphasizing sports and warrior ideals and railing against the “feminization” of the culture.

Tolstoy might be said to represent a “vegetable Christianity”—seeking harmony with nature and turning away from all forms of violence, including the eating of meat. In “The First Step,” an 1891 essay on diet and ethical commitment, he characterized the prevailing religious attitude toward food:

I remember how, with pride at his originality, an Evangelical preacher, who was attacking monastic asceticism, once said to me “Ours is not a Christianity of fasting and privations, but of beefsteaks.” Christianity, or virtue in general—and beefsteaks!

While he confessed himself “not horrified by this association,” it is only because “there is no bad odor, no sound, no monstrosity, to which man cannot become so accustomed that he ceases to remark what would strike a man unaccustomed to it.” The killing and eating of animals, Tolstoy came to believe, is a horror to which—like war and serfdom—his culture had grown far too accustomed. Like many an animal rights activist today, Tolstoy conveyed his horror of meat-eating by describing a slaughterhouse in detail, concluding:

[I]f he be really and seriously seeking to live a good life, the first thing from which he will abstain will always be the use of animal food, because, to say nothing of the excitation of the passions caused by such food, its use is simply immoral, as it involves the performance of an act which is contrary to the moral feeling—killing.

[W]e cannot pretend that we do not know this. We are not ostriches, and cannot believe that if we refuse to look at what we do not wish to see, it will not exist.… [Y]oung, kind, undepraved people—especially women and girls—without knowing how it logically follows, feel that virtue is incompatible with beefsteaks, and, as soon as they wish to be good, give up eating flesh.

The idea of vegetarianism of course preceded Tolstoy by hundreds of years of Hindu and Buddhist practice. And its growing popularity in Europe and America preceded him as well. “Tolstoy became an outspoken vegetarian at the age of 50,” writes Sam Pavlenko, “after meeting the positivist and vegetarian William Frey, who, according to Tolstoy’s son Sergei Lvovich, visited the great writer in the autumn of 1885.” Tolstoy’s dietary stance fit in with what Charlotte Alston describes as an “increasingly organized” international vegetarian movement taking shape in the late nineteenth century.

Like Tolstoy in “The First Step,” proponents of vegetarianism argued not only against cruelty to animals, but also against “the brutalization of those who worked in the meat industry, as butchers, slaughtermen, and even shepherds and drovers.” But vegetarianism was only one part of Tolstoy’s religious philosophy, which also included chastity, temperance, the rejection of private property, and “a complete refusal to participate in violence or coercion of any kind.” This marked his dietary practice as distinct from many contemporaries. Tolstoy and his followers “made the link between vegetarianism and a wider humanitarianism explicit.”

“How was it possible,” Alston summarizes, “to regard the killing of animals for food as evil, but not to condemn the killing of men through war and capital punishment? Not all members of the vegetarian movement agreed.” Some saw “no connection between the questions of war and diet.” Tolstoy’s philosophical argument against all forms of violence was not original to him, but it resonated all over the world with those who saw him as a shining example, including his two daughters and eventually his wife Sophia, who all adopted the practice of vegetarianism. A book of their recipes was published in 1874, and adapted by Pavlenko for his Leo Tolstoy: A Vegetarian’s Tale. (See one example here—a family recipe for macaroni and cheese.)

In her study Tolstoy and His Disciples, Alston details the Russian great’s wide influence through not only his diet but the totality of his spiritual practices and unique political and religious views. Interestingly, unlike many animal rights activists of his day and ours, Tolstoy refused to endorse legislation to punish animal cruelty, believing that punishment would only result in the perpetuation of violence. “Non-violence, non-resistance and brotherhood were the principles that lay at the basis of Tolstoyan vegetarianism,” she observes, “and while these principles meant that Tolstoyans cooperated closely with vegetarians, they also kept them in many ways apart.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In the second stanza of “How to Be a Poet,” Wendell Berry wrote: “There are no unsacred places; / there are only sacred places / and desecrated places.” When it comes to preserving important historical locations, such as monuments, parks, and buildings, a new interactive public art installation asks, “what happens when preservation itself is endangered?”

The Sacred Ordinary is an initiative organized by 1504, a production studio based in Birmingham that emphasizes in-depth storytelling to connect people with meaningful, human-focused services and experiences. The participatory artwork is presented in collaboration with the National Parks Conservation Association, which aims to protect U.S. national parks for future generations.

In early 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that mandated the removal of some National Park Service signage relating to slavery, the LGBTQ+ community, climate change, and more, a move that erases histories inextricable from the nation’s identity. (The current administration has also blocked millions in funding for numerous parks and disrupted services.)

In Birmingham, the Civil Rights District is formally designated a national monument, comprising neighborhoods that Black people historically called home and where Jim Crow laws authorized segregation until the 1960s. The Civil Rights Movement reached a nexus here when activists Fred Shuttlesworth, Martin Luther King, Jr., and Ralph Abernathy, among many others, organized nonviolent marches in 1963, known today as the Birmingham Campaign. Police turned their dogs on demonstrators and used fire hoses on children. A bombing at a Baptist church killed four young Black girls.

The Sacred Ordinary venerates access to things most of us take for granted: the ability to shop at any store, attend the nearest school, walk around any neighborhood, and sit at the front of the bus. The exhibition is installed around-the-clock, but by day, elements of the installation comprise vintage yet mundane objects that one typically walks by without giving a second thought.

A huge midcentury television rests on an open lawn, and a red newspaper vending box for The Birmingham News, which ceased its print publication in 2012, advertises 25 cents per copy. Additional sites include a characteristically blue U.S. Postal Service mailbox and a walk-in telephone booth. Sheets of paper with tear-off tabs posted around town invite participants to learn more by texting a phone number. If you text “HERE” to the number, you’ll be directed to a starting point and an otherwise nondescript yellow fire hydrant.

In scavenger-hunt style, visitors are prompted to enter the year stamped on the unit, and if it’s between 5 and 8 p.m., the sequence of texted prompts doubles as a multimedia self-guided tour of Birmingham’s Civil Rights District like you’ve never seen it: the television screen, mailbox, phone booth, and more begin to glow once the sun has set.

“Birmingham, Alabama, is known around the world for such places—sites of civil rights history that many regard as sacred and that connect us to something larger than ourselves. But today, that memory is endangered,” 1504 says in a statement. “Aging infrastructure, the passing of a generation of foot soldiers, and federal efforts to erase chapters of American history raise an urgent question: if institutions alone cannot sustain history, what role can the public play in caring for sacred sites?”

Rather than center primarily on signage, The Sacred Ordinary focuses on objects associated with civic life in the mid-20th century, evoking collective memories and providing touchpoints for younger generations for whom boxy televisions, printed newspapers, and telephone booths feel distant from today’s experiences. Emblematic of the way news and information spread before the internet and smartphones, the objects confront visitors with not only the realities of how people organized and communicated during that time but also how those memories are preserved today. Even without didactics, objects and places carry meaning that no one can simply delete.

The tour opens with a narration by actor André Holland, who played a fundamental role in preserving a historic theater in nearby Bessemer, Alabama, and 1504 has dedicated the installation to Birmingham-based artist Joe Minter. The Sacred Ordinary continues nightly through December 13, with accompanying guided walks and other programs scheduled in the meantime. Learn more on the project’s website, and explore the studio’s work on Instagram. You might also be interested in “The Praise House,” directed by 1504’s Tyler Jones.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Celestial filmmaker Seán Doran is back with a new project that interprets stellar snapshots from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. The footage-like video tours the sun and reveals its fiery surface complete with brilliant solar flares, all depicted in a distinctive crimson.

To create the film, Doran attributed various pinks and reds to different wavelengths, creating an alluring interpretation of the fiery orb. Doran stitched together NASA’s captures, or more accurately, he says, the images were “conformed, repaired, graded, blended, rescaled and retimed” into a seamless film. “Crimson Star” is one of several astral projects he’s undertaken in recent years, and you can keep up with his latest works on YouTube. (via Kottke)

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Refugees at Moria Camp, Lesbos, Greece, July 2015. Photo by Georgios Makkas/Panos

is a former taxi driver and currently an accidental professor of anthropology at Stockholm University in Sweden. His recent books include the co-edited collections Waiting and the Temporalities of Irregular Migration (2020) and Seeing Like a Smuggler: Borders from Below (2022).

In 1986, I was 19 and behind bars in a small prison on the border between Iran and Pakistan. I had been arrested while attempting to cross the border irregularly into Pakistan. Everyone I met in that prison had been detained in connection with the border. It was a small space, the cells overcrowded and unsanitary, but it held an extraordinary diversity of people: local smugglers, large-scale drug-traffickers, undocumented migrant workers, and refugees; Iranians, Afghans, Pakistanis, as well as Baluch men whose communities had crossed these lands freely for generations but who were now being punished for violating the territorial order of the nation-state. Multiple languages were spoken at once. Different histories, geographies and ways of inhabiting the world converged within the same confined space.

Yet we all shared one thing. We had refused, for different reasons, to respect the border. The state saw us through a single imaginary: as criminals, trespassers or illegal bodies to be contained. We, however, were animated by different imaginations. Each of us had imagined a life that exceeded the border and acted upon that imagination. In that sense, the prison did not simply contain border-crossers; it brought together people whose aspirations had collided with the territorial imaginary of the nation-state.

That prison experience was perhaps one reason I became a scholar of borders. It remains, even today, the most important school of border studies I have ever attended. The conversations in the cells and during brief moments in the prison yard revolved around borders; how they operated, how they were enforced and, above all, how they might be circumvented. The prison became an unlikely site of knowledge-production: not simply the sharing of survival strategies but the enactment of an imagination that paid no heed to prison walls or state borders.

M any years later, in a prison north of Stockholm, I interviewed a human smuggler who told me he saw himself as an architect: ‘I design a journey, like an architect designs a building,’ he said. The comparison stayed with me. Architects imagine and design structures that do not yet exist. Their work begins with the capacity to visualise what is not yet visible. In a similar way, smugglers design border crossings that, from the perspective of the state, would be impossible. A smuggler’s work consists of imagining routes where borders appear closed, creating connections where states impose separation, and envisioning possibilities for mobility when people are immobilised by borders. A smuggler speculates on possibilities in seemingly impossible situations. Seen this way, the smuggler’s ‘architecture’ is an enactment of an imagination that refuses the state imaginary expressed through borders.

The parallels between human smuggling and architecture helped me understand the relationship between imagination, fugitivity and knowledge-production. While fugitivity and imagination are oriented toward the future, toward not-yet-realised possibilities, state power often relies on backward-looking imaginaries grounded in myths of shared blood, origin and belonging. States are hostile to this relationship because it exposes borders as political constructions that can be reimagined, negotiated and crossed. Like capitalism, the nation-state depends upon such imaginaries to stabilise its claims to totality, making it difficult to imagine a world beyond capitalism and the nation-state system.

Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat

All around us, across the world, people are being confined, displaced, silenced and rendered disposable, in service of imaginaries that seek to define the limits of life, mobility and freedom. We live in a conjunctural moment shaped by the convergence of two dark forces: borderless wars that destroy lives, produce death and generate displacement, and endless borders that deny mobility to those seeking survival. Together, they produce fugitive lives and fugitive bodies. But they also produce fugitive imagination, the irreducible capacity to envision and enact life beyond the worlds that seek to contain it.

Philosophers often define imagination as the capacity to hold present in the mind what is absent from sensory perception. It is also the capacity to envision alternative ways of organising social reality. Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat. The state-centric imaginary presents history as coherent, and intact through symbols, narratives and rituals. The capacity to disrupt the hegemony of state imaginaries is therefore criminalised, suppressed and persecuted. In this sense, fugitivity is inseparable from imagination.

A fugitive is someone fleeing harsh institutions and conditions. The fugitive is an outlaw: a person hiding from a hostile law. Historically, the term referred to enslaved people’s resistance to slavery, its dehumanising logic, and the political economy built upon the extraction of uncompensated labour to maximise profits from cash crops like cotton, tobacco and sugar. Fugitivity was a response to captivity and, as such, an act of liberation, not only from the brutal material conditions of enslavement, but also from the imposed image of the enslaved subject produced by racist ideology. Fugitivity is a way of escaping and a way of knowing.

When Frederick Douglass, one of the most important figures in the 19th-century struggle for African American freedom and civil rights, began learning to read, his enslaver Hugh Auld forbade it, declaring that, if Douglass learned to read, ‘there would be no keeping him’. Once capable of reading, Auld argued, Douglass would inevitably desire to write, and ‘this accomplished, he will be running away with himself.’

This phrase is striking. It suggests a distinction between the enslaved person and the enslaved body. To ‘run away with oneself’ is not simply to flee physically; it is to reclaim one’s imagination and humanity. Under slavery, where Black bodies were turned into capital, fugitivity was criminalised as theft. The fugitive was pursued by law because they were perceived to have stolen property from their enslaver: their own body. In reality, they were reclaiming what had first been stolen from them. If the captivity of the body depends upon the captivity of the mind, then the emancipation of consciousness becomes a precondition for bodily liberation. Such emancipation engenders new subjectivities and creates the conditions for imagining what previously appeared impossible: life beyond chains, borders and confinement. Auld’s anxiety over Douglass’s literacy reflected precisely this logic. His fear was not simply the loss of labour, but the emergence of a subject who would not obey the racial imaginary; ‘he will be running away with himself.’

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agricultural past remains just within living memory. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with pictures of the animals it comes from, sometimes dressed in chef’s garb and cheerfully serving up the very dishes they’re about to become.) Things were different in medieval Europe, where animals were both a necessity and a potential danger. History records many instances of serious harm done to humans by horses, bulls, and especially pigs, who seem to have had a particular tendency to turn on children.

Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhuman act, a term that, in these cases, applies more than figuratively. As for the fate of the violently offending animal, we might imagine that it would be summarily slaughtered, but between the tenth and eighteenth centuries — and especially in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — it might well have been brought into a courtroom first. Though other creatures had already been subject to legal proceedings for quite some time, “the earliest recorded pig trial took place in Fontenay-aux-Roses, just outside Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexander Lee at History Today. “By the early fifteenth century, however, they had become established practice throughout Normandy and the Île-de-France,” eventually spreading beyond the border to Italy, Germany, and the Low Countries.

“As contemporary students of the Corpus iuris civilis knew, it was a basic principle of Roman law that animals could not be culpable,” Lee adds. “Lacking reason, they were incapable of harboring criminal intent and hence could not be guilty of a crime.” But in un-Roman northern France, “the administration of secular justice was still largely the concern of local seigneurs and was governed predominantly by custom rather than statute.” Thus sustained, animal trials served purposes beyond simple punishment. “For medieval people, the world was created by God in a very logical way, with animals created first, in order to serve and help human beings who were created in the image of God,” says University of Liverpool medieval European monster expert Damian Kempf, quoted in Popular Science by Anne Ewbank. In that worldview, trying and executing a pig could “restore what was broken.”

Unlike domestic animals, according to Sonya Vatomsky at JSTOR Daily, destructive mice, beetles, snails, weevils, and other vermin would be sent to ecclesiastical tribunals. “Despite being unlikely candidates for Catholicism, such creatures were punished with excommunication, not execution,” she writes, since casting them out of God’s domain would allow humans to exterminate them with peace of mind. Vatomsky also quotes economist Peter T. Leeson’s theory that the Catholic Church tried more animals when people got lax about tithing, with the aim of “bolstering citizens’ belief in the validity of Church punishments for tithe evasion.” Putting animals on trial may now strike us as grotesque, but like any alien-seeming episode of history, it also reveals the beliefs on which a past society operated — a mode of analysis that gets one wondering how far the modern United States is from giving them the right to sue.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Taught by historian Marci Shore, “European Intellectual History Since Nietzsche” surveys the story of modern thought, from the late 18th century to the late 20th.

Along the way, the course explores major trends in modern European thought: Marxism-Leninism, psychoanalysis, expressionism, structuralism, phenomenology, existentialism, anti-politics, and deconstruction. Intellectual figures covered in the course include Nietzsche, Lenin, Kafka, Freud, Husserl, de Beauvoir, Heidegger, Arendt, Adorno, Sartre, Girard, Foucault, Derrida, and Havel.

You can watch all 25 lectures above. Or find them on YouTube and Apple Podcasts. Explore the course handouts here.

“European Intellectual History Since Nietzsche” will be added to our collection, 1,700 Free Online Courses from Top Universities.

Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together. When researchers began mapping real-world networks in the 1990s – from the World Wide Web to Hollywood actors linked by films – they found that wildly different systems shared architectural features that their components alone could not explain. This suggested common organizing principles for how networks form and develop.

In this episode, two of the pioneers of network science – Albert-László Barabási and co-host Steven Strogatz – discuss how the field took shape, the ideas that underpin it, and why this is more than graph theory under a different name. The conversation then turns to health and nutrition. Disease-related genes cluster in “network neighborhoods”, Barabási explains, which may help identify better drug targets and predict which patients will respond to which drugs. That work led him to his Foodome project , which catalogs the molecules found in the food we eat and asks what they do inside our cells. By his count, around 135,000 compounds lie outside conventional nutrition, which concerns itself mainly with energy, building blocks, and vitamins. These compounds, which he calls the “dark matter of nutrition,” and their effects on the body are only beginning to be understood.

Listen on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , TuneIn or your favorite podcasting app, or you can stream it from Quanta .

LEVIN: A podcast… where… you can’t make me laugh, okay. A podcast from Quanta Magazine where we explore some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.

STROGATZ: Well, hey, Janna, I’m gonna take you back in a time warp to the 1990s. Do you wanna go there with me?

STROGATZ: There was a trend back then, where people would play a game that they called Six Degrees of Separation.

STROGATZ: Right. So if people don’t remember, Kevin Bacon, he was in a lot of movies and a game developed around him where you would name an actor, whoever, Marlon Brando or James Dean, and then you have to figure out a path of co-stars. You know, Marlon Brando was in such and such movie with somebody who was in a movie with Kevin Bacon. In that case, we would say Marlon Brando was two steps away. He had a Bacon number of two.

LEVIN: [ Laughs ] Right. Now, this though has some actual mathematical underpinnings. And as I remember, you did substantial work on some of this, how we’re all connected and how the world is smaller than we think, how that happens. You know, how do you… Do you know the guy Joe from Chicago? And you’re like, “Of course I know Joe.” Right?

STROGATZ: Well, it is true. My student Duncan Watts and I got very interested in the math of Six Degrees of Separation, like what would a network have to be like to have that property? And around that time, when we published our paper, soon after we heard from Malcolm Gladwell before he was really famous as Malcolm Gladwell, and he wanted to talk about this idea, and he ended up writing an article that was called Six Degrees of Lois Weisberg.

STROGATZ: Yeah, that’s the point. Everybody knows Lois. Lois knew everyone in Chicago and all over the place.

And so, we all know that there are these connectors in our networks, and that’s actually what we’re gonna be hearing about to some extent in this upcoming interview with László Barabási.

So, he is a network scientist at Northeastern University. He’s also got an appointment with Harvard Medical School and with the Central European University in Budapest, Hungary. And he has been looking at the role of what he calls hubs. You know, these outsized Lois Weisberg-like nodes in a network that seem to have a tremendous number of connections and the effect that they have on the behavior of the network as a result.

LEVIN: This probably has application for other complex systems than just human social systems?

items.summary: After decades of bickering about which molecules came first, a new generation of scientists is rethinking what life was, is, and could be. The post The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology first appeared on Quanta Magazine

items.cleanReaderHtml:

Scientists are homing in on the 200 million years after the conditions for life emerged on Earth but before our most ancient single-celled ancestor appeared.

A round 4.6 billion years ago, some 9 billion years after the birth of the universe, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the familiar blinding ball in our sky. Scraps of leftover material collided and accreted into the planets of the solar system, including our own. For the next few hundred million years, Earth was a hellish, molten landscape bombarded by meteorites. As it started to cool, water pooled into vast, acidic oceans. The days, half as long as today’s, passed under pink carbon dioxide skies. But life wasn’t around to sense any of it. Until it was.

Around 300 million years into the existence of our solar system, conditions on Earth were right for a great chemical experiment to begin. Molecules entangled themselves in self-sustaining, self-reproducing loops. Over time, these systems became more complex. At some point, they had come to life.

Life invented new ways to move, and to capture, store, and use energy. It began to sense, respond to, and change its environment. It communicated, ate some of its neighbors and lived inside others, and formed complex, dynamic communities. Through cycles of birth, reproduction, and death; catastrophe; and bursts of evolution, it persisted and then thrived, taking over every corner of the planet.

Scientists engaged with the origins of life are asking not just what life is, but what it does — on an archaic world, in a modern lab, or somewhere beyond our solar system.

Then, at some point, life gained a sense of itself, a reflective intelligence with the existential curiosity to ask: Where did we come from? For tens of thousands of years, we have pondered and probed the origins of life: Monks have meditated, philosophers have argued, lovers have mused, and parents have patiently answered their kids’ questions.

“Go back in human history, go back to the Neanderthals, go back 30,000 years,” said William Schopf , a paleobiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles, “and one of the things you will see is that human beings have been wrestling with this question.”

By the mid-20th century, it became possible to probe life’s origins through chemistry, molecular biology, and genetics. Hypotheses exploded. Scientists clashed over which type of molecule — RNA , lipids , proteins , and metabolites are prime suspects — could have started it all. The arguments have gone on for so long, without resolution or unifying insight, that some experts have considered the field to be in crisis.

“There’s nothing more exciting for a scientific field than a moment of crisis,” said Betül Kaçar , an astrobiologist and evolutionary biologist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison. “That’s when I think breakthroughs happen.”

Life’s origins are not purely a chemistry problem. “It’s not a linear reaction. … There’s no single E = mc 2 and that’s origin of life’s formula,” said Betül Kaçar, an astrobiologist and evolutionary biologist. “This is biology; it doesn’t follow any rules. That’s what makes it so sophisticated and exciting.”

A new wave of origins-of-life researchers, fed up with the tradition of bickering, have unshackled themselves from the idea that a single type of molecule started it all. Their open-minded approach has coincided with a change in scientific understanding. Experiments have shown that the precursors to many of life’s ingredients may have formed easily under the conditions on early Earth. What is harder to explain is how these molecular processes became a stable evolutionary system continuous with the vast diversity of life we see on the planet today. During life’s earliest days, these processes came together to store and pass on information, both consistently and imperfectly enough to allow the same living lineage to persist for billions of years on an ever-changing planet.

To study the emergence of lifelike biochemical systems, biologists are now pushing backward into the past from the living world with new genetic tricks, while chemists are pushing forward from the nonliving world with new and strange mixtures of molecules. And by combining tools from chemistry and biology, synthetic biologists are embracing informed speculation and probing novel biological systems that may not have ever existed. Scientists now engaged with the origins of life are asking not just what life is, but what it does — on an archaic world, in a lab dish, or somewhere beyond our atmosphere.

The Soviet biochemist Alexander Oparin was one of the founders of the field. “Like two parties of workers boring from the two opposite ends of a tunnel, they [chemists and biologists] are working towards the same goal,” he wrote in a pamphlet in 1924. “The work has already gone a long way and very, very soon the last barriers between the living and the dead will crumble under the attack of patient and powerful scientific thought.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The artist Nora Abbott, a Pitjantjatjara and Western Arrernte woman, paints scenes from Central Australia, including the family histories she came to know while caring for her maternal grandfather. Among them is the story of Lewis Harold Bell Lasseter, who went in search of what he believed to be an abundant ‘gold reef’ in the region in 1930. In this short animation adapted from Abbott’s paintings, she recalls Lasseter’s final days from the perspective of her grandfather and his people, the An̲angu, who were initially terrified of this stranger, but eventually sought to help him. While Lasseter’s fateful journey and ultimate death in the bush are a staple of settler Australian folklore, Abbott’s colourfully rendered account tells the story from the An̲angu point of view, centred on a peculiar outsider ‘searching for minerals’ and losing his way.

Icebergs (1893-95) by Robert E Peary. Courtesy the Met Museum , New York

is associate professor in the Department of Religion and Philosophy at Hong Kong Baptist University. He is the author of Personal Ontology: Mystery and Its Consequences (2024), The Methodology of Metaphysics (2026) and Why Is There Something Rather Than Nothing? The Fundamental Problem of Ontology (2026).

Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the issue in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when properly considered. This very obvious fact about the world – that things exist – can shift from seeming mundane and trivial to very surprising, even downright weird. Ludwig Wittgenstein expressed this astonishment when he wrote in his Tractatus (1921): ‘Not how the world is, is the mystical, but that it is.’ Arthur Schopenhauer in 1818 called the question ‘an unfathomable and always disquieting riddle’. And the Rigveda , one of the world’s oldest surviving religious texts, suggests that even the ‘overseer’ ( adhyakṣaḥ ) of the cosmos might not know the answer. Sheer existence is baffling.

Philosophers continue to discuss the question today, but there isn’t any consensus about the answer. Some have suggested that it’s the sort of question that couldn’t possibly have an answer. In 1973, the German philosopher Carl Hempel wrote:

His idea is that if you were trying to explain why, for instance, any penguins at all exist, then you couldn’t appeal to a penguin in your explanation – after all, that penguin is one of the things you are trying to explain. Similarly, if we’re looking for an explanation for why anything at all exists, then our explanation cannot appeal to an existing thing, since that existing thing is one of the things we are trying to explain. But Hempel thinks that there couldn’t possibly be any other sort of explanation for why anything exists, since any explanation for why something exists has to appeal to some other existing thing.

One response to Hempel’s concern is to go ahead and do what he claimed can’t possibly be done: offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, an explanation that ‘does not assume the existence of something’. Many philosophers have attempted to do just that. But there is something wrong with these explanations.

W hy might we expect there to be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing in the first place? Leibniz thought there must be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing because, as he put it, nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. It is this thought that lies behind much of the astonishment people have expressed at the fact that there is something rather than nothing.

A world in which nothing exists is how we should expect the world to be if it takes what would, by our usual criteria, be its most probable state. What I have in mind here is Ockham’s Razor . Simpler accounts of the world are more likely to be correct than complex ones. For example, consider all the traits shared among the species alive today. Whales and humans have similar bone structures, despite the fact that they live in very different environments. One of Charles Darwin’s key insights was that, while it might conceivably have been true that a creator just happened to want these various species to have similar traits, despite their different environments and lifestyles, it is so much simpler to suppose that they share those traits because those traits are derived from a common ancestor. And the simplicity itself of that explanation gives us an excellent reason to think that the common traits are derived from a common ancestor. We constantly rely on the assumption that the simplest account of the world compatible with our evidence is most likely to be correct. This is something we do in science as well as in everyday life.

Many of the proposed explanations for why there is something rather than nothing that have been offered in the past do not address the apparent fact that nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. The proposed explanations say that there is such-and-such a reason for why there is something rather than nothing, but they do nothing to address the thought that we should antecedently expect there to be nothing because, if there had been nothing, then reality would have been so much simpler.

There would have been a whole lot of non-ontological truths even if nothing had existed

What I’d like to do here is kill two birds with one stone: to offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, which simultaneously dissolves the suspicion that nothing would have been so much simpler than something. This also happens to be, as far as I can tell, a new explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, and new explanations are hard to come by given the antiquity of the question.

I would like to start with the important insight that there are truths that are not truths about existing things. Since they are not truths about existing things, we’ll call them ‘non-ontological’ truths. Contrast these with ‘ontological’ truths – truths that are about existing things, like the truth that Earth orbits the Sun, or that there are more trees in the world than there are dogs. The observation that there are non-ontological truths is an insight expressed by other philosophers puzzled by the question of why there is something rather than nothing. For example, in a number of publications, the philosopher John Leslie has argued that there is something rather than nothing simply because it is good for there to be something rather than nothing. Setting aside whether this is a successful explanation, note that it appeals to a non-ontological truth: even if there was nothing, then there would have still been the truth that reality was less good than it could have been. And that does seem plausible.

Once we notice that there are non-ontological truths, we can see on reflection that there would have been a whole lot of them even if nothing had existed. Here are a few examples:

Again, these are just a few examples. I could list many others. Admittedly, it’s mysterious how we know about these non-ontological truths. Since they don’t concern existing things, it’s surprising that our cognitive faculties can ‘get a grip’ on them, in the way that they can get a grip on objects with which we can interact (eg, the dog in front of me that I can see with my eyes and pet with my hand).

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A mercenary and miscreant, the Swiss Renaissance artist Urs Graf lived the violence and vice he summoned on his drafting table. Miya Tokumitsu introduces us to his astonishing drawings of soldiers and sex workers, and finds an impotent melancholy within these often nightmarish scenes.

Urs Graf the Elder, Prostitute Inviting Love , 1514 — Source .

Many artists draw ably; a rarefied few draw with an animating touch that can imbue a single line with meaning, mood, and character. Some soft scribbles and scratches become an owl with a scowl full of menace and cynicism. A thatch of quick slashes forms a clump of grass that radiates the carnal energy of the figure before it, a young woman offering herself for sex. 1 These marks appear in the work of Urs Graf the Elder (ca. 1485–ca. 1528), one of the great maestros of the pen, who possessed one of the wilder imaginations of the sixteenth century. A mysterious and troubling figure, Graf bequeathed to the world a set of astonishing drawings filled with erotic-melancholic imagery : virile soldiers and wily prostitutes, with a supporting cast of satyrs, lecherous monks, and fools. His iconography reflects the context of Swiss martial culture during the Italian Wars of the early sixteenth century, interpreted via his self-consciously bizarre sensibility. Yet his compositions continue to fascinate due to their punchy, graphic style and their audacious visual meditations on sex and death. Centuries before Freud, Graf plumbed the far reaches of these fundamental human drives.

Born in Solothurn, Switzerland, around 1485, Graf was taught by his goldsmith father, Hug, from whom he presumably learned the fundamentals of design and draftsmanship in addition to metalwork techniques. As a young man, between 1503 and 1509, he worked as a designer of book illustrations in Strasbourg and as a goldsmith in Zürich, finally settling in Basel and establishing his own enterprise. In 1511, he married Sibylla von Brunn; their son was born the following year. While establishing his artistic career and family, Graf fought in at least four military campaigns as a Swiss mercenary, or Reisläufer : he set out to Rome with a troop from his hometown of Solothurn in 1511; joined a Basel expedition to Dijon in 1513; fought French and German forces at Marignano in 1515; and in 1521 marched on Milan and Bicocca. 2

Urs Graf the Elder, Standard-Bearer with His Page , 1516 — Source .

Urs Graf the Elder, Pyramus and Thisbe , 1525 — Source .

At home, Graf was a notorious and incorrigible miscreant. He was censured and jailed numerous times for transgressions that included: spousal battery; adultery and patronizing prostitutes; mocking and slandering local citizens including a priest, tailor, and coachmaker; and assaulting locals, often without apparent provocation. In 1518, he fled the city following an assault so violent that his victim was permanently disabled. He was permitted to return the following year, however, as the city was in need of a die-cutter for its mint and Graf’s talents proved too compelling for them to cancel him permanently. 3 Basel’s publishers, too, continued to seek his services as an illustrator. From 1527, documentation of Graf’s activity evaporates. Sibylla remarried in October 1528 (one hopes, to a nicer man), suggesting that Graf had died or disappeared from Basel by then. 4 That year, Graf would have been about forty-three years old.

Somehow, amid all his decamping for battle and local troublemaking, Graf managed to be a prolific and successful artist. If he were active today, he would surely qualify as a “multihyphenate creator”, skilled as he was in book illustration and single-sheet woodcut design, metalwork, stained glass production, engraving, and drawing. Graf also experimented in the novel technique of etching, which emerged around the 1510s. From his goldsmith training, he developed a keen sense of design and ornamental composition that disposed him favorably to the book publishers of Basel and Strasbourg who employed him as an illustrator. (That he evidently worked quickly was surely a boon, too.) Drawing was the medium in which Graf was truly groundbreaking, however. 5 He employed an eye-catching graphic style to depict vernacular subjects in transgressive scenarios; it is a visual strategy that remains effective still today, evident in the work of Kara Walker, who also reformulates figures and tropes from popular media like silhouettes and minstrel shows into nightmarish scenes.

Urs Graf the Elder, Woman with Child and Fool , 1525 — Source .

In one of Graf’s many drawings of sex work , a mercenary soldier and prostitute stand together as a couple, in a half embrace. This is no love match; wearing a weary expression, the woman fondles the man’s purse, which dangles from his neck just above his codpiece and a perpendicularly hanging sword. Gazing down at the coin bundle being evaluated, the man extends an open hand in a gesture of negotiation. Each person has something the other wants as well as their own risks to weigh. If rejected, the man suffers sexual humiliation. By issuing such a rejection, the woman risks provoking revenge in the form of battery and rape — a possibility suggested by the man’s burly physique and ample, priapic weaponry. She could become pregnant out of wedlock, a condition with its own jeopardies and burdens. The specter of venereal disease looms over both figures. The least harmful outcome seems a mutually agreeable exchange of sex for money in which both protagonists depart, health intact. But given that women in the sex trade at this time usually entered it for lack of other means of survival, such transactions were hardly made on equal terms. 6 Nevertheless, this woman has apparently made the best of her lot in life, as evidenced by her keys, heavy purse, and dagger — all common visual signifiers of a head of household during the early modern period. She is not entirely without power or authority.

Urs Graf the Elder, Soldier and Young Woman in a Landscape , ca. 1500–28 — Source .

Graf’s imagery opens a view onto the heady and hazard-filled world of the Swiss mercenary, a figure emblematic of political and social upheaval at the dawn of the modern era. It was the mercenary’s daily labor that implemented epochal shifts in war- and statecraft that emerged during the Renaissance. The Italian Wars (a yearslong mêlée that entangled Swiss, French, Italian, and German forces) engendered new methods of warfare that entailed larger-than-ever armies of professional troops, mostly infantry, skilled in modern weapons and tactics. 7 A two-sheet panoramic woodcut by Graf’s German contemporary, Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528), pictures a sixteenth-century fortress siege, complete with large, disciplined troop formations, heavy artillery, and the logistical coordination of massive baggage trains. This is not the kind of operation that can be carried out by a labor force significantly padded with pressed peasant boys and village layabouts. It required large numbers of competent, battle-hardened soldiers. This new way of making war, defined by the simultaneous professionalization and expansion of armies, came at an unprecedented financial cost, producing another now-familiar piece of state machinery: sprawling, sophisticated taxation and credit systems. 8

Albrecht Dürer, The Siege of a Fortress , date unknown — Source .

This modern warcraft shook up the Swiss social order. In 1477, Swiss pikemen surged into continental renown following their victory over Charles the Bold and his Burgundian knights in the Battle of Nancy. 9 Armies from all over Western Europe were keen to fill their ranks with Swiss recruits. Rather suddenly, a Swiss youth from the countryside, who had previously faced a future of cowherding, now had the opportunity to enjoy travel, adventure, sexual hijinks, and potential riches in the form of war booty. All he had to do was enlist with the recruiter passing through town. In fact, enough Swiss cowherds enlisted that their German battlefield antagonists, called Landsknechte (“servants of the land”), coined a panoply of cow-themed epithets to describe them: Kuhmäuler (cow mouths), Kuhbuben (cow boys), Kuhschwäntze (cow tails). 10 Mercenary culture quickly embedded itself into Swiss society, and it became common for men, urban and rural, to dabble in warfare for a campaign or two. 11 It was not only the uneducated or destitute who answered the calls to fight. Graf’s artist compatriot, Niklaus Manuel (ca. 1484–1530), also did some turns as a mercenary. In addition to his pursuits in the visual arts, Manuel was a playwright and member of the Bern civic council from 1510 until his death — a true Renaissance man. 12

items.title: How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life
items.author: Jake Buehler
items.summary: Energetic pathways that make and break complex molecules are critical to all life. It’s even possible that these self-sustaining cycles could have been key at life’s beginning. The post How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life first appeared on Quanta Magazine
